Tech Report: Why anything exists

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3462 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Writing in 1714, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz asked: ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’ Philosophers have long wondered why the Universe exists, but Leibniz is credited with framing the glitch in precisely these terms.
  • In a recent development, philosophers continue to discuss the question today, but there isn’t any consensus about the answer.
  • According to recent reports, his idea is that if you were trying to explain why, for instance, any penguins at all exist, then you couldn’t appeal to a penguin in your explanation – after all, that penguin is one of the things you are trying to explain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Writing in 1714, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz asked: ‘Why is there something rather than nothing?’ Philosophers have long wondered why the Universe exists, but Leibniz is credited with framing the glitch in precisely these terms. The question is head-spinning when properly considered. This very obvious fact about the world – that things exist – can shift from seeming mundane and trivial to very surprising, even downright weird. Ludwig Wittgenstein expressed this astonishment when he wrote in his Tractatus (1921): ‘Not how the world is, is the mystical, but that it is.’ Arthur Schopenhauer in 1818 called the question ‘an unfathomable and always disquieting riddle’. And the Rigveda, one of the world’s oldest surviving religious texts, suggests that even the ‘overseer’ (adhyakṣaḥ) of the cosmos might not know the answer. Sheer existence is baffling.

In a recent development, philosophers continue to discuss the question today, but there isn’t any consensus about the answer. Some have suggested that it’s the sort of question that couldn’t possibly have an answer. In 1973, the German philosopher Carl Hempel wrote:.

According to recent reports, his idea is that if you were trying to explain why, for instance, any penguins at all exist, then you couldn’t appeal to a penguin in your explanation – after all, that penguin is one of the things you are trying to explain. Similarly, if we’re looking for an explanation for why anything at all exists, then our explanation cannot appeal to an existing thing, since that existing thing is one of the things we are trying to explain. But Hempel thinks that there couldn’t possibly be any other sort of explanation for why anything exists, since any explanation for why something exists has to appeal to some other existing thing.

Industry observers note that one response to Hempel’s concern is to go ahead and do what he claimed can’t possibly be done: offer an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, an explanation that ‘does not assume the existence of something’. Many philosophers have attempted to do just that. But there is something wrong with these explanations.

Why might we expect there to be an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing in the first place? Leibniz thought there must be an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing because, as he put it, nothing would have been so much ‘simpler and easier’ than something. It is this thought that lies behind much of the astonishment people have expressed at the fact that there is something rather than nothing.

Sources indicate that A world in which nothing exists is how we should expect the world to be if it takes what would, by our usual criteria, be its most probable state. What I have in mind here is Ockham’s Razor. Simpler accounts of the world are more likely to be correct than complex ones. For example, consider all the traits shared among the species alive today. Whales and humans have similar bone structures, despite the fact that they live in very different environments. One of Charles Darwin’s key insights was that, while it might conceivably have been true that a creator just happened to want these various species to have similar traits, despite their different environments and lifestyles, it is so much simpler to suppose that they share those traits because those traits are derived from a common ancestor. And the simplicity itself of that explanation gives us an excellent reason to think that the common traits are derived from a common ancestor. We constantly rely on the assumption that the simplest account of the world compatible with our evidence is most likely to be correct. This is something we do in science as well as in everyday life.

Many of the proposed explanations for why there is something rather than nothing that have been offered in the past do not address the apparent fact that nothing would have been so much ‘simpler and easier’ than something. The proposed explanations say that there is such-and-such a reason for why there is something rather than nothing, but they do nothing to address the thought that we should antecedently expect there to be nothing because, if there had been nothing, then reality would have been so much simpler.

There would have been a whole lot of non-ontological truths even if nothing had existed.

Recent findings suggest that what I’d like to do here is kill two birds with one stone: to offer an explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, which simultaneously dissolves the suspicion that nothing would have been so much simpler than something. This also happens to be, as far as I can tell, a new explanation for why there is something rather than nothing, and new explanations are hard to come by given the antiquity of the question.

I would like to start with the notable insight that there are truths that are not truths about existing things. Since they are not truths about existing things, we’ll call them ‘non-ontological’ truths. Contrast these with ‘ontological’ truths – truths that are about existing things, like the truth that Earth orbits the Sun, or that there are more trees in the world than there are dogs. The observation that there are non-ontological truths is an insight expressed by other philosophers puzzled by the question of why there is something rather than nothing. For example, in a number of publications, the philosopher John Leslie has argued that there is something rather than nothing simply because it is good for there to be something rather than nothing. Setting aside whether this is a successful explanation, note that it appeals to a non-ontological truth: even if there was nothing, then there would have still been the truth that reality was less good than it could have been. And that does seem plausible.

Once we notice that there are non-ontological truths, we can see on reflection that there would have been a whole lot of them even if nothing had existed. Here are a few examples:.

Again, these are just a few examples. I could list many others. Admittedly, it’s mysterious how we know about these non-ontological truths. Since they don’t concern existing things, it’s surprising that our cognitive faculties can ‘get a grip’ on them, in the way that they can get a grip on objects with which we can interact (eg, the dog in front of me that I can see with my eyes and pet with my hand).

There can conceivably be possible worlds – possible ways for reality to be – that are not merely ways things could be.

An immediate objection is that if there were truly nothing then there would not be any non-ontological truths either. A truly empty world would have nothing at all, including truths of any sort. The philosopher Tyron Goldschmidt expresses this thought when he writes in The Puzzle of Existence (2013) that the question of why any beings at all exist is:.

But I don’t think this is right. This view assumes that, in asking why anything at all exists, we are asking why there are any truths at all (in Goldschmidt’s terms, ‘why any world obtains’). That is not what we are asking. We are looking for an explanation for existence specifically. We are not asking why there are truths rather than no truths. That would, as Goldschmidt himself notes, be a confused question to ask, since there isn’t any alternative to there being truths, not even an impossible alternative. ‘A situation in which nothing is true’ doesn’t describe a situation, not even an impossible situation, since descriptions of a situation tell us what is or would be true were that situation to happen. With the concept of non-ontological truths, we can also see that there can conceivably be possible worlds – possible ways for reality to be – that are not merely ways things could be. In those empty worlds there would be truths, but no things.

According to recent reports, many non-ontological truths would still be true even if nothing existed because they are necessarily true, if true at all. For example, recall modus ponens. That logical rule couldn’t help but be true, whether or not anything exists. The same holds for many of the other non-ontological truths, such as truths regarding what is possible and impossible, mathematical truths, and moral truths.

Some of these non-ontological truths are more controversial than others. But you don’t have to buy into every non-ontological truth to see that a possible world in which nothing exists would be more complex than it seems at first glance. When we think of complexity we normally think of the complexity of things and their properties and behaviours. But there is this whole other sort of complexity that is more abstract: complexity with respect to non-ontological truths.

Even if a possible world in which nothing exists might be more complex than we initially thought, it doesn’t follow that Leibniz was wrong when he noted that it is simpler for nothing to exist than for something to exist. After all, you might think that if something exists this would leave us with all those non-ontological truths cited above as well as ontological truths about the things that exist. But postulating something new can simplify our overall picture of reality if the new thing can explain a great deal that would otherwise remain unexplained.

Sources indicate that A possible world in which something exists may very well simplify matters if one or more of the existing things could explain why the non-ontological truths are true. This is similar to how Darwin simplified our account of biological reality by postulating the existence of something we didn’t previously believe in: a common ancestor. So if something of the right sort exists, this might make reality simpler than if nothing at all exists, if the existing thing can explain why many of the non-ontological truths are true. The simpler that existing thing is, and the wider the range of non-ontological truths it can explain, the simpler our overall account of reality will be. But what sort of existing thing might do the trick? Three possibilities naturally suggest themselves, though I don’t claim that these three options are exhaustive.

First, God is a natural candidate. Here I have in mind the sort of God we find in the world’s major monotheistic religions, all-powerful, all-knowing and so on. The feature of theism most vital for our purposes is the idea that God’s nature and decisions are supposed to ultimately explain many aspects of reality. It is God’s status as reality’s explanatory bedrock that makes God a natural candidate for explaining various non-ontological truths. For example, if there is a God, then God’s decisions would explain various negative existential truths. Mechagodzilla doesn’t exist because Mechagodzilla just isn’t one of the things God wanted to create, or allow to be created.

Sources indicate that divine command theorists such as William of Ockham (of Ockham’s Razor fame) explain moral truths in terms of God’s commands – an act is good or bad because God commands it to be. René Descartes notoriously claimed that God decrees which logical and mathematical truths are true. These truths could not be otherwise – they are necessary – but that too is only because God decided they can’t be otherwise. There is also a case to be made that God is a particularly simple being. If that’s right, then our overall account of reality might end up being simple if God explains why many non-ontological truths are true. There is the traditional doctrine of divine simplicity, endorsed by prominent Jewish thinkers such as Maimonides, Christian thinkers such as Thomas Aquinas, and Islamic thinkers such as Ibn Sina. According to this view, there are no distinctions at all within God, either between God’s attributes, or between God and God’s attributes. Over the past several decades, the philosopher Richard Swinburne has argued in detail for a more modest way of understanding the idea that God is a very simple being, and so theism is a very simple hypothesis. The basic idea, which I don’t have the space to discuss in detail, is that many of God’s attributes (omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness, etc) are ultimately derivable from one or two of God’s attributes, and those attributes fit together in a neat and tidy manner.

Industry observers note that here is a second option if the God explanation doesn’t appeal. Many of the non-ontological truths might be explained by a natural (that is, non-supernatural) object that explains why the Universe has many of the properties it has. Suppose that the Universe originated in a cosmic singularity, an object of infinite density. The state of the initial singularity would, given how the laws of nature dictate the Universe evolves over time, explain why various negative existential truths are true. This is because the Universe’s initial conditions plus the laws will result in the Universe’s history taking one course rather than another, one that either does or does not include the existence of various particular things in it. Even non-deterministic laws may dictate that the existence of certain things is very improbable, given the Universe’s initial conditions.

The actual world, though filled with existing things, may for all we know be the simplest possible world.

Some philosophers think that truths regarding what is possible and impossible in the broadest sense are also explained by the properties had by an initial singularity. The idea is that what’s possible and impossible is grounded in which states of the Universe can result from the evolution of the initial singularity, given how the laws of nature say the Universe will evolve over time. If some state of the Universe can in principle result from the initial singularity and the laws, then it’s possible, but if it can’t result then it is strictly impossible, as impossible as a round square. In fact, on this view that’s what makes round squares impossible. But would an initial singularity give us a particularly simple explanation for various non-ontological truths? The philosopher Quentin Smith argued that an initial cosmic singularity is as simple as it gets, since an initial singularity would have had no spatial extension, no mass (at least on some models), and would not have been governed by any physical laws. So it’s certainly a candidate.

It has been revealed that A third possibility is that we humans make many of the non-ontological truths true. And, with various degrees of plausibility, many of the non-ontological truths cited earlier have been attributed by some philosopher or other to our decisions, conventions, practices or whatever. For example, moral anti-realists such as Sharon Street think that there are moral truths, but that they are made true by our attitudes, conventions or practices (or the attitudes we would have in ideal conditions). Logical conventionalists such as Jared Warren contend that logical truths are a result of our linguistic practices. Mathematical intuitionists such as the mathematician L E J Brouwer think that mathematical truths are mentally constructed.

There are surely more possibilities than these three. But, confining our attention to these three options – God, singularity, human beings – is one of them clearly preferable to the others? It’s difficult to say. There are many non-ontological truths, and some non-ontological truths may be more plausibly explained by an existing thing than would other non-ontological truths. It is difficult to see how some of these explanations would work; I’ve never seen anyone claim that an initial singularity might explain which moral truths are true. And a full evaluation of the three options would require a detailed examination of the relative merits of the various explanations on offer. We would have to take a look at each of the versions of divine command theory and human-centred moral anti-realism on offer, and see if any of them seem plausible on closer inspection. That being said, the first two options (God, singularity) do seem to fare better than the third option with respect to simplicity. They propose to explain lots of non-ontological truths by appealing to one existing thing, an existing thing that might be very simple. By contrast, if we try to explain various non-ontological truths by appeal to human beings, we don’t seem to have a very simple explanation. Human beings are complex objects. There are also a lot of human beings. Are the non-ontological truths explained by some of them, or all of them? How would we reconcile conflicting human attitudes or practices that might result in contradictory non-ontological truths? It’s hard to see how we might come up with an elegant or simple way of accounting for how that’s all supposed to work.

Industry observers note that we can leave further speculation regarding the details to another occasion. The main point is this: if we can posit some existing thing that is simple enough, and capable of explaining a wide-enough range of the non-ontological truths, we might very well end up with an account of reality in which one or more things exist, and yet which is simpler than an account of reality in which nothing exists. In fact, despite how counterintuitive it seems at first, the actual world, though filled with existing things, may for all we know be the simplest possible world, if it has a sufficiently simple explanatory foundation. In that case, Leibniz would have been incorrect when he said that nothing would have been ‘simpler and easier’ than something. If we found ourselves surprised that reality didn’t take its simplest and seemingly most probable state, one in which nothing exists, that sense of surprise should dissolve.

Suppose that if something of the right sort exists, then that would be simpler than if nothing at all existed. Would this fact explain why there is something rather than nothing? Presumably it would only if we think that reality is the way it is because of how simple it is. In other words, we would have to think that reality is somehow striving toward simplicity, so that, if the world is as simple as it can be, this is because it is as simple as it can be. You shouldn’t oppose this idea on the grounds that our world is very complex, since, as I’ve emphasised, that complexity might be accounted for in terms of a very simple explanatory starting point.

It has been revealed that A more serious worry is that, even if our reason for thinking that something is true is because it is simpler (remember Ockham’s Razor), it doesn’t follow that the thing itself is true because it is simpler. The reason we think the various species have a common ancestor is because this hypothesis is the simplest explanation of the evidence. But that simplicity isn’t what makes it true that there is that common ancestor.

It has been revealed that we should question this assumption that simplicity never explains why some state of affairs comes about. The idea that sometimes reality takes a simpler form because it is simpler is more defensible than it might first seem. It would have the benefit of explaining why simplicity is a guide to truth (that is, why we should accept principles such as Ockham’s Razor), a methodological practice followed in both science and everyday life, but which is notoriously hard to justify. What’s more, many of us follow Leibniz in being puzzled at the fact that reality didn’t take what seems at first to be its simplest form, wherein nothing exists. We tend to think that if nothing had existed, and if this would have in fact been the simplest way for reality to be, then nothing would have existed precisely because nothing was so much simpler than something.

Industry observers note that my argument flips this line of reasoning on its head. We should expect reality to be simple, and for all we can tell that’s exactly what we find. There being something rather than nothing shouldn’t surprise us if that’s the simplest way for reality to be. That wouldn’t explain everything. Supposing that reality somehow strives for simplicity, for example, we might very well wonder why that’s the case. It won’t work to say that reality strives for simplicity because that’s the simplest way for reality to work, as that would be a circular explanation. So, even if my extremely speculative proposal is correct, we’d still be left with a lot of mystery. Out of the infinite number of ways for reality to be, why did it turn out this way? That’s still a baffling question, even if we conclude that one of reality’s features, that things exist, might turn out to be less baffling than it initially seems.

The 2026 Chefs of the Year

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1379 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five U.S. chefs making waves in their communities with compelling menus.

According to recent reports, if you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Each of the chefs featured in our new national Chef of the Year category made news in a major way. But their most recent projects are just one part of their story.

Recent findings suggest that this year we celebrate five chefs who are making an impact both on the city where they cook and on the larger culinary conversation. — Missy Frederick, editorial director.

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

San Francisco diners became acquainted with powerhouse couple Laura and Sayat Ozyilmaz through their championing of Eastern Mediterranean cuisine at Dalida. That restaurant told the story of Sayat’s upbringing and influences in Istanbul, Turkey, opening in 2023 inside a historic building within the lush environs of the Presidio and earning critical acclaim for the duo’s cooking.

In a recent development, in the years since, diners came to know Laura outside of Dalida. She completed an impressive run on Top Chef in 2024, where viewers saw her deftly plant one foot in Mediterranean food and another in Mexican cuisine, showcasing her skill in both fields throughout the season. With the 2026 debut of the Ozyilmazes’ restaurant Maria Isabel, the food feels like an even fuller expression of Laura’s heritage and personal history.

Named after Laura’s sister (Maria) and her mother (Isabel), the restaurant steeps in Mexican matriarchy, highlighting female winemakers, ceramics made by Mexican producers, and indigenous Mexican ingredients. The menu channels Laura’s upbringing in Guerrero and her family’s Sinaloan roots, as recounted through mariscos and maiz, moles and salsa macha. The ceviche Acapulqueño reimagines the Fanta- and ketchup-laden version instead with marigold flowers and preserved Seville oranges dressing tender shrimp and raw scallop; petals — and three fried shrimp heads — adorn the top. Duck enmoladas showcase the power of mole negro against a seasonal mole (sometimes a peach manchamanteles, other times a rhubarb rendition, but always compelling). Chochoyotes, a lesser-seen dish in San Francisco, demonstrates the restaurant’s ability to apply masa in different ways — in this case, dumplings — while harnessing the earthy flavor of huitlacoche. Maria Isabel is both a conduit for diners to connect with complex Mexican flavors and a view into Laura’s vision of the Mexico of her past and future. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF.

Chef Carlos Delgado’s meteoric rise in D.C. began in 2022 with the opening of tiny tasting room Causa, located in Shaw, where he sends diners on a seafaring voyage along the Peruvian coastline and into the Andes he grew up around, and its accompanying upstairs pisco destination Bar Amazonia. His meticulous sourcing and culinary skills quickly drew critical acclaim.

2026 might be the Lima native’s biggest year yet: His breakout project, Maru San, commanded instant Capitol Hill buzz upon opening in February for its orchestra of Nikkei-style hand rolls, sashimi, and other polished seafood plates he and fellow José Andrés alum Simon Lam pass across a 25-seat black marble counter under a massive pink octopus mural, as his favorite tropical house blasts in the background. A rare few get to sample the restaurant’s elaborate tasting menu full of ingredients like high-end uni and dry-aged fish; reservations for the 15-course feast are nearly impossible to get.

It has been revealed that the ambitious chef, at 36, isn’t afraid to stretch in many directions. He linked up with the Eaternity Group last year to give the Mediterranean-themed La Vie a needed menu makeover at D.C.’s Wharf development — meanwhile, at least one more Maru San is in the works elsewhere in D.C.

Sounds a lot like his former mentor: Before Causa, Delgado honed his craft under José Andrés as the longtime executive chef at Penn Quarter’s Peruvian mainstay China Chilcano. They still text frequently. — Tierney Plumb, Northeast editor.

According to recent reports, while Amir Hajimaleki has had American-leaning restaurants in Austin for well over a decade, he hasn’t had the opportunity to fully express himself as an Iranian-born, Texas-raised chef. That is until he opened Roya, his most personal restaurant and a project that has been in the works for more than eight years. Here, he manifests the depth and diversity of Persian cuisine, a bold feat for the middle of Texas. The space, designed with his brother Ali Hajimaleki, feels transportive with intricate tile mosaics, burnished gold and dark blue hues, and delicate chandeliers.

There’s been an electric energy to the Philly restaurant scene in recent years. The city, ever the underdog, has long punched above its weight; now, the rest of the world has come to the same realization. Amid this buzz, two newer restaurants have outrun the shadow cast by the city’s substantial names: Cambodian noodle house Mawn, which opened in 2023, and Southeast Asian oyster house and raw bar Sao, which opened last September.

At their helm is the slick, stylish Phila Lorn. The restaurants he runs with his wife Rachel feel singular, blending the influences of his Philadelphia upbringing with his Cambodian background in food that feels playfully free and emboldened by a lack of boundaries between cuisines. At Mawn, funnel cake meets coconut macaroons, and vinegar peppers enhance scallops in red curry. At Sao, the crispy rice in the nam khao salad, which features Italian sausage, feels analogous to arancini. Tuna carpaccio is served with crispy shallots and jalapeños, then cured in lime until it picks up the aura of the bowls of beef pho on Washington Avenue.

Hear Lorn talk, with his South Philly-bred bravado (and requisite uses of “jawn”) giving him a commanding presence, and it’s clear that the city’s culinary community is listening, rallying, and getting stoked to eat more of his food. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Recent findings suggest that tucson-based chef Aaron Lopez had a vision that started in his small California city of El Centro, an agricultural city near the U.S.-Mexico border. There, he hatched a blueprint to create a menu imbued with the techniques and flavors of the Sonoran Desert that spans northern Mexico, Arizona, and southeastern California. Trained at top kitchens in Los Angeles and beyond, Lopez researched by going deep into the desert, armed with a camera and his wits. A year later, he and his wife June Chee carried the project to Tucson, a larger venue still deeply embedded in the desert, but with a fresh audience.

In a recent development, inside the high-ceilinged, brick-walled downtown space, Ursa serves as a hushed gallery for Lopez and his team’s $150 tasting menu, which merges Indigenous cooking techniques with foraged and locally farmed ingredients. Barrel fruit (a yellow cactus) topped with the tang of pickled chiltepin leaves is the first bite, a luscious treat you may never see on a European plate. Quail breast arrives on a metal skewer dressed in pickled yucca, hovering over a jujube broth like a quiet offering. Goat roasted in agave, pit barbacoa-style, is unveiled tableside and served over softened tepary beans.

It has been revealed that at every turn, with no extraneous adornments, the kitchen lets the produce and meats boast their innate nature. Lopez eschews conventional comfort, reimagining a meal of cactus, corn, sunflower tea, and beans as true luxuries, and the results are evocative and powerful. His message — seeing the value and beauty of this landscape, its people, its ingredients, and the way it all comes through the cooking — is the luscious pith of the cactus you find beneath the surface of the American Southwest. — Matthew Kang, correspondent.

The 2026 Restaurant Dishes of the Year

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1312 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From an earthy curry crab callaloo dip to a plate of pickled walleye cheeks, these were editors’ most memorable bites.
  • Our editors ate in hundreds of restaurants across the country this year, but certain dishes left a lasting impression, and we’re recognizing them in this new national Eater Award category.
  • It has been revealed that from a textbook execution of the ubiquitous 2026 entree — roast chicken — to an innovative fish preparation offering Midwestern diners a new way to experience a familiar ingredient, these dishes are all worth celebrating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From an earthy curry crab callaloo dip to a plate of pickled walleye cheeks, these were editors’ most memorable bites.

Our editors ate in hundreds of restaurants across the country this year, but certain dishes left a lasting impression, and we’re recognizing them in this new national Eater Award category.

It has been revealed that from a textbook execution of the ubiquitous 2026 entree — roast chicken — to an innovative fish preparation offering Midwestern diners a new way to experience a familiar ingredient, these dishes are all worth celebrating. — Missy Frederick, editorial director.

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

Sources indicate that when experiencing a five-course tasting menu ($145), I wasn’t expecting toast to be a main attraction. But even with competition from luxurious courses featuring everything from a complex Hokkaido scallop to an assertive charred rib-eye with peaches, All Well’s puffed grain toast left a lasting impression.

After three years at two-Michelin-starred Oriole, Larry Feldmeier partnered with Noah Sandoval, fellow Oriole alum and James Beard winner for Best Chef: Great Lakes, to open the ambitious West Loop restaurant All Well, which offers both a la carte bar options and the aforementioned tasting; the toast is only available as part of the latter experience.

The dish arrives to the table amplified with nutty buckwheat butter sweetened with honey, the backdrop for a pasta stuffed with triple-cream Délice de Bourgogne and a cauldron of salty chicken brodo. You’ll dive into the pasta, of course, using the bread to sop up the rich beurre blanc. Like a performer waiting in the wings for their monologue, the puffed grain toast takes center stage. The toast effectively offsets the creaminess and saltiness of the rest of the dish, but can stand on its own even without the accompanying pasta. Its subtle sweetness almost acts as a mid-meal dessert, a distinctive break in a seamless dinner you don’t quite want to end. — Isaiah Reynolds, audience editor.

The only thing about Oklahoma City that feels even vaguely reminiscent of the Caribbean is the sheet-pan-flat horizon. And yet inside a gaping industrial dining room downtown, there’s Dougla Kitchen, where diners sip fruity rum drinks out of plastic bags and acclaimed chef Andrew Black digs deep in his past to bring OKC locals a taste of his Indo-Jamaican upbringing. I fully admit this Midwestern-born, California-raised girl doesn’t encounter ruddy callaloo greens as often as she’d like (my hunch is neither do most Oklahomans). No matter. What Black manages to do with this deceiving pile of greenish-brown mush, dank with hand-picked crab and sparkling with curry spices, translates the soul of Caribbean home cooking in a single scoop. I didn’t know it was possible to be overwhelmed by a sense memory from a life that’s not your own, but this heady appetizer does that, served with a side of crisp taro chips and worth lingering over all afternoon with a couple of Red Stripes. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

According to recent reports, to understand California cuisine in 2026, look no further than Henrietta, a neighborhood bistro that has struck a just-right balance of precision and ingenuity while imbuing a feeling of nostalgia that begs locals and travelers alike to return. The restaurant’s intentions come across most clearly in its roast chicken, served as a just-salty-enough half chicken hunked into handheld pieces with deep, smoky char marks. The prize chicken pile gets tucked onto a plate alongside a scorched lemon half and a heaping, chicory-heavy Caesar panzanella blanketed under a layer of Parmesan that could be a snowcap on a stretch of the San Gabriel Mountains. With the chicken, Henrietta nods to forebears (namely San Francisco’s Zuni), while making the dish its own with a Baja-born Caesar salad that feels distinctly Los Angeles, dotted with torn fistfuls of bread from the neighboring local Clark Street Bakery. Of course, 2026 continues to be the year of the Great Chickening, where roast chicken has become many a restaurant’s calling card — and an easy way into the cultural cache. In Los Angeles alone, Sqirl (with its latest dinner menu) and Pasjoli have both put out progressive, near-intoxicating spins on the dish, but Henrietta’s has lodged itself into the collective imagination with its brazen simplicity. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest.

Sources indicate that the striking cantaloupe and verjus terrine at Nashville’s Junior offers a glimpse into the minds of chef Philip Krajeck and chef de cuisine Brian Mejia, the duo behind the high-technique kitchen. A “terrine” slice arrives with pieces of cantaloupe suspended in a clear gelatin made with verjus, the pressed juice of unripened grapes. One corner is covered in tiny, diced cubes of cantaloupe dressed in citrus-forward turmeric oil; another gets draped in chamomile-steeped cream. The mix of textures and flavors comes together in a dynamic symphony: the bright, acidic cubes of summer-ripened fruit against the calming mellowness of chamomile and gelatin layers that meld cantaloupe juice sweetness with crisp verjus.

The dessert’s structural elegance, which highlights a French variety of melon grown by a local farmer, may not immediately reveal its full complexity: Clear gelatin features a layer of clarified cantaloupe juice with encased melon slices, stacked between two layers of verjus gelatin. The melon gets compressed to intensify its flavors. Somehow, Junior managed to make Jell-O cool again — and dare I say, even sophisticated? — an example of Junior’s steady confidence that makes the restaurant an irresistible experience. — Dianne de Guzman, lead editor, Eater SF.

Though people outside the Midwest may not be familiar with freshwater whitefish walleye, there it’s a classic comfort food, a staple of Lenten fish fries, state fair booths, and Lake Erie fishermen’s freezer stashes. At Rosy, chef Vinnie Cimino leans on that familiarity to help convince his customers to experience a beloved ingredient in an entirely upcoming way. Pickled walleye cheeks ($17) have been a recurring staple — if a fleeting one — on Rosy’s Eastern European-leaning menu since the restaurant opened in February 2026. Kate’s Fish in Cleveland’s historic West Side Market provides walleye filets for sister restaurant Cordelia; when breaking down and fileting each fish, the fishmongers save the cheeks until they have a formidable stash. About every three weeks, Rosy can offer pickled walleye cheeks for around four days at a time. It’s a thoughtful move for sustainability, but also for succulence, as fish cheeks are a prized cut for their luscious texture.

It has been revealed that cimino conceived the dish as a nod to Jewish fish-pickling practices (for me, the results also brought to mind a tender ceviche). Seasonal vegetables are pickled with lemon — an earlier version invoked German-style potato salad, spring brought asparagus, and, when I went in June, bell pepper, carrot, and dill were in the mix. They’re then combined with the cheeks, which get a separate hot-pickling treatment involving red wine vinegar, salt, sugar, bay leaf, peppercorns, and coriander. “People really gravitate toward it,” Cimino says. “We’ve built up a great trust with our diners.” While the dish won’t be replacing fried walleye at area fish fries anytime soon, Cimino feels proud that when at Rosy, diners have been more than willing to go along with him for the ride. — MF.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Walk down Pink Street in Lisbon’s Cais do Sodré and you’ll eventually find a door that looks like it has secrets. Pensão Amor building is a former brothel that has been transformed into a surprising space in Lisbon's port district.

Cais do Sodré was once the sailors’ quarter, where seamen fresh off the boats mingled with writers, fado singers, artists, prostitutes and the occasional spy. Pensão Amor takes that cast of characters and gives them a party.

According to recent reports, the bar is a riot of velvet, red light, and cheerful mischief. On any given night, you might catch burlesque, pole dancing, live music, poetry, or theater, sometimes all in the same week. Nobody here is trying to hide what the building used to be. They hung it on the wall.

In a recent development, other surprise is upstairs. In 2023, the old brothel floors reopened as Madam’s Lodge, a 22-room hotel with a twist: every room has its own invented backstory. Screenwriter and director Roger Mor wrote each one, drawing on archival research and objects tied to the building and the neighborhood.

Illustrator Nuno Saraiva drew the characters and left his mark across the building, so even the walls seem to have opinions. Some rooms also come with pole dancing bars, strategically placed mirrors, bathtubs made for two, and minibars stocked with adult goodies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ever dreamed of visiting a cozy Christmas village in Austria or a luxury ski resort in the Alps? Really, who hasn't? The cost of such a trip is often way beyond an average family's budget, so most of us believe that this must remain a dream. But there is another way to get your perfect winter vacation in the U.S.

According to recent reports, several towns nestled within American mountain ranges have been designed to mimic the European villages that tourists love, allowing those of us who aren't able to fly internationally to still partake in our very own winter wonderland. These towns have all the charm and whimsy of the European originals, so your dream winter trip could be a reality without spending any euros.

Recent findings suggest that nearly 30 miles outside of Salt Lake City, Midway is Utah's "Little Switzerland." In the 1850s, Swiss and German immigrants settled in the area, influencing everything from the architecture to cultural celebrations. A stay at the Zermatt Utah Resort and Spa will have you questioning whether you're not actually in a fancy European ski lodge.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of skiing, Midway's Soldier Hollow was a site for the 2002 Winter Olympics and is now a great place to ski, snowboard, snowshoe, or tube sled. There is also Swiss influence in the food, with plenty of chocolate and artisanal cheeses that taste as authentic as if they were made in a small Alpine village available.

In a recent development, leavenworth almost became a ghost town after the railroad was rerouted, and the townspeople were desperate to find ways to attract tourists. In the 1960s, Leavenworth was completely redone to emulate a Bavarian village in Germany. The entire downtown area was rebuilt with chalets and cozy shops filled with German schnitzel, ale, and goods.

During the winter, Leavenworth has two festivals that have made it world-famous: Christmastown and the Winter Karneval. These festivals are filled with lights, music, and events like ice sculpting and a gingerbread house contest. They also have a reindeer farm, a nutcracker museum, and bands dressed in lederhosen playing German folk songs.

According to recent reports, boasting the title of "First American Destination Ski Resort," Sun Valley, Idaho, has been famous since 1936. Ernest Hemingway even wrote For Whom the Bell Tolls while staying at the Sun Valley Resort, and many other celebrities came to ski at the place that rivaled Europe's resorts.

In a recent development, you can enjoy the Winter Wonderland festival between Thanksgiving and New Year's, where they have a holiday market, ice skating, sleigh rides, a tree lighting ceremony, and so much more. And, of course there's top-notch ski slopes on both Bald Mountain and Dollar Mountain.

Stowe Mountain Resort was built just one year too late to be the first American ski resort, but it still earned its namesake the nickname "Ski Capital of the East." The slopes are some of the best in the Northeast U.S., and the skyride gondolas provide a magnificent view of Vermont. Other winter activities in Stowe include dog-sledding, ice skating, ice climbing, and snowshoeing.

Another lodge in Stowe is famous for its Austrian style, having been founded by the von Trapp family themselves. After the real-life events on which The Sound of Music was based occurred, the von Trapp family made it to America and opened the von Trapp Family Lodge and Resort and von Trapp Brewing. If you're looking for an authentic Austrian feel, or want to see the American hills come alive, Stowe is the place to visit.

According to recent reports, the artist Nora Abbott, a Pitjantjatjara and Western Arrernte woman, paints scenes from Central Australia, including the family histories she came to know while caring for her maternal grandfather. Among them is the story of Lewis Harold Bell Lasseter, who went in search of what he believed to be an abundant ‘gold reef’ in the region in 1930. In this short animation adapted from Abbott’s paintings, she recalls Lasseter’s final days from the perspective of her grandfather and his people, the An̲angu, who were initially terrified of this stranger, but eventually sought to help him. While Lasseter’s fateful journey and ultimate death in the bush are a staple of settler Australian folklore, Abbott’s colourfully rendered account tells the story from the An̲angu point of view, centred on a peculiar outsider ‘searching for minerals’ and losing his way.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Precision pastries are sweeping the nation. These bakers are leading the charge.

If there’s one thing we’ve noticed over the past several years, it’s how much bakeries have stepped up their game.

Some embody a personal expression of a baker’s identity, while others push the envelope beyond expected flavor combinations; all excel at a time when “little treat” culture is at its peak. — Missy Frederick, editorial director.

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

If one upcoming place in Chicago needs no further hype, it is Bad Butter. You’ll know you’re there when you spot the line cascading out of the whitewashed storefront along West Cortland Street, a queue that doesn’t let up until the pastry case is empty. Formerly a head baker at Soho House Chicago, Dan Koester was stuck at home like the rest of us in 2020, handing off excess home-baked sourdough loaves to friends and family and making some available for free pickup. After he was officially laid off that summer, he rolled out his own online bakery business, earning a massive following along the way.

One residency at the Emily Hotel later, Koester debuted his Bucktown bakery, demonstrating the full range of his skill. Still warm, charred, and dimpled flats of focaccia showered with scallion furikake rest on its shelves. Impossibly crisp and exquisitely laminated twice-baked almond croissants burst with subtle, aromatic almond paste. A spicy harissa monkey bread with a cloudlike texture is cooled by a pool of creamy labneh drizzled with silky olive oil.

The bakery’s menu has breadth and also manages to arc with the season. Customers snake along the floor waiting their turn to claim a towering cruffin, dusted in fine grains of sugar and piped full of ginger plum jam, or a seasonal tart piled with plump, lacquered blueberries. A pastry box filled with these confections is well worth the wait. — Brenna Houck, dining editorial manager.

Born as an underground dinner party operated out of Karla Subero Pittol’s Echo Park garage, Chainsaw finally got its own digs in November 2025 in the form of a lively cafe in Melrose Hill, an unquestionably gentrifying neighborhood that has become home to some of Los Angeles’s best independent restaurants. At the cafe, Subero Pittol channels her Venezuelan heritage through a menu of arepas plump with beans, limey guasacaca, and cheese; a Venezuelan hot dog (“perro caliente”) buoyed by an acidic slaw; and her bracingly tart passionfruit-lime icebox pie, which commands a cult following all its own.

Sources indicate that stepping into Chainsaw feels like you could be in Subero Pittol’s own kitchen as she greets regulars and newcomers as if they are old friends. Customers study a handwritten menu that changes daily — it doesn’t help to come in too attached to any one dish (save the ever-present icebox pie) when you may get tempted by another. The cafe’s impact on Los Angeles feels clear in the near-constant crowds that hover outside, reading their newspapers over an espresso or tucking into the latest of Subero Pittol’s ideas, such as a full English breakfast served for a single day. In a city lacking in untamed Venezuelan cooking, Chainsaw offers a home for Subero Pittol to celebrate the cuisine in a way that feels distinctly Los Angeles. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest.

With both Afghan and Latin American influences, Diljān gives Upcoming Yorkers a bakery with a point of view and innumerable reasons to become a regular. Ali Zaman and Mohamed Ghiasi, owners of Astoria’s Little Flower Cafe, teamed up with Bryan Ford, Honduran American baker and cookbook author, to conceptualize the bakery, now perched on a corner near Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn Heights.

Their combined talent makes for some of the city’s most compelling baked goods. For the Saffron Shah, laminated pastry holds delicate saffron cream in the shape of a crescent, an vital Islamic symbol. Halwa tops the sticky bun, while a swirl of samosa pastry wraps halal lamb under a dusting of powdered sugar. Don’t miss the enormous Afghan flatbread crowned by toppings such as halal beef bacon with scallions or sour cherry cream cheese. The team has also branched into pizzas topped with cheese and Afghan cumin, kofta kebabs, or beef pepperoni. Look for specials like the flan with cardamom-poached apricots and conchas stuffed with firni, a rice pudding. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater Latest York.

Recent findings suggest that san Francisco’s pastry game is stronger and more competitive than ever before, and Parachute Bakery steps to the forefront of a crowded field with a mix of patisserie standards and seasonal standouts. At his Ferry Building bakery, pastry chef Nasir Armar marries his fine dining training, honed at Michelin-starred Sorrel and Saison, with flavors that make everyone sit up and take notice (and snap a food photo or two for their socials).

Industry observers note that vegetables and savory complements are given their own footing on the menu. Stalks of grilled asparagus shine in a baton-shaped croissant shell, with fennel jam, sheep’s milk ricotta, and ramp pesto alongside them; one brief, bordering-on-gimmicky croissant got piped with clam chowder, a reference to the soup in a bread bowl famously served on the city’s wharf. Even potato-laden samosas and bright tomato shakshuka get interpreted into pastry form. Parachute succeeds with its experimental vision, a hype well-earned that leaves fans clamoring for what they’ll come up with next. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF.

Welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it. Each food diary follows one anonymous reader’s week of expenses related to groceries, restaurant meals, coffee runs, and every bite in between. In this time of rising food costs, The Receipt reveals how folks—from different cities, with different incomes, on different schedules—are figuring out their food budgets.

Industry observers note that in today's Receipt, we follow a 43-year-old server and drag queen in Toronto, Ontario. Keep reading for his receipts.

What is your occupation? Server, Drag Queen.

Sources indicate that what city and state do you live in? Toronto, ON.

Recent findings suggest that what is your annual salary, if you have one? Girl, I have no idea. Waiting tables brings in around $60K CAN, and performing in bars, nightclubs and drag brunches probably makes me another $3K, but all those sweat and glitter covered bills get stuffed under a mattress, so who knows?

In a recent development, how much is one paycheck, after taxes? Let’s call it an even thousand dollars.

How often are you paid? (e.g., weekly) Weekly or bi-weekly.

What are your approximate fixed monthly expenses beyond food? (i.e., rent, subscriptions, bills).

Recent findings suggest that do you follow a certain diet or have dietary restrictions? I avoid salt and gluten as much as possible.

In a recent development, what are the grocery staples you always buy, if any? Eggs, gluten-free pasta, bananas, bone broth, greens, yogurt. I almost always have boiled eggs ready in the fridge, a tub of yogurt, some dark berries, and bananas to keep me fueled up. If I’m going to cook, it’s pasta or meat and veggies.

It has been revealed that how often in a week do you dine out versus cook at home? I work in an upscale Italian restaurant and the food is exceptional. I eat there 3 or 4 times a week and have the cholesterol levels to prove it. At 50% off any menu items (minus the $128 porterhouse steak) it’s a bargain to eat delicious, mostly healthy cooked meals. I love going out socially or alone, and do so almost weekly.

How often in a week did you dine out while growing up? Once a month? Rural Alberta didn’t have a ton of dining out choices.

Industry observers note that how often in a week did your parents or guardians cook at home? Daily. My mom’s (and occasionally my dad’s) cooking was excellent. Nothing fancy, but a real meat-and-potatoes type menu that kept us going.

10 a.m. My annual sinus infection came early, and I’ve been sick since Saturday. I’m trying to break my morning caffeine habit, but today I’m too lazy and run down. I hydrate with lemon water while sipping an Americano with brown sugar. Between the coffee and the illness I don’t have much of an appetite. I forage on peanut butter and pumpkin seeds while shuffling around my apartment.

Recent findings suggest that 4 p.m. A thought occurs to me: Let’s heal this body with some miso and wasabi. I order sushi from Kibo down the street. It’s take-out, so I am forced to don clothing and walk down the street. I pick up 2-for-1 dynamite rolls, chicken gyoza dumplings, miso soup, the obligatory green salad that comes with it all. and a spicy salmon combo. $44.

It has been revealed that as I’m feeling sorry for myself on my walk back home, I stop at the corner store for a bottle of Blake Boulevard Sauvignon Blanc. $21.

It has been revealed that 10 a.m. I know that I have a shift at the restaurant today, so I'm holding my head up and pretending that I'm not at death's door. A banana and blueberry yogurt provide the gas I need to leave the house to get provisions.

In a recent development, we’re out of coffee beans! I have two espresso machines because I am a complete coffee snob. Machine number 1, my favorite, is a DeLonghi manual espresso maker, a tall, silver tower with a handle on the side. I grind my own beans for this. Machine number 2 is a Nespresso Virtuo. It requires aluminum pods stuffed with coffee. It’s sleek and makes a lovely crema, but it’s never hot enough for me. The pods vary between $1.12 and $1.50 each.

According to recent reports, on the way home I stop in at St. Clair Avenue Fruit Market for some of my usuals: bok choy, celery, dates, rapini, bananas, and a container of feta, for fun. $31.75.

In a recent development, 3 p.m. Before work I load up on cold meds even though they make me feel like a bobble head. Somewhere between 4PM and 7PM I ask my chef to sneak me some arancini to avoid passing out while bringing some nice folks their wine and dinner. Our arancini are filled with mozzarella, rolled in a saffron risotto and plated with tomato sauce. Retail $24, but for me it’s $12.

Recent findings suggest that 10 a.m. Americano, brown sugar, lemon water. I have a friend coming in from out of town and she is fully aware how ill I am, and I feel as though she may need a snack after her 2+ hour drive, so I pop down to another cute hot spot on my street, Le Bleu. I may or may not also have a huge crush on the owner, Iman. I pick up vegan baklava, vegan banana bread, a Caprese sandwich for her and prosciutto for me. I try to make small talk with Iman while he packs up my order, but he’s so handsome I end up muttering and mumbling my thank yous while I stumble out the door. $25.76.

6 p.m. Reservations for 2 at a vegetarian restaurant, Planta, Toronto, in Yorkville. I am not a vegetarian. I had mid to low expectations. Guys, this place was incredible.

Delicious regular and zero-proof cocktails. A “Cosmic Colada” for me: Coconut water, lemon, blueberry and pineapple. For my friend: the Tokyo Blossom made with sake, gin, lychee liquor and grapefruit tonic.

According to recent reports, the unagi eggplant was so good I almost ordered a second one; we also ordered spicy tuna roll (some kind of juiced-up watermelon substitution), miso soup, and bang bang broccoli. I ordered a chocolate brownie and a sticky toffee pudding for dessert—the latter was so massive it was almost comical. They also stuffed an entire ice cream cone full of vanilla ice cream upside down onto my pudding. I finished about a quarter of it.

It has been revealed that after she leaves and the day progresses I realize I am in no shape to work. Thankfully someone takes my serving shift so I don’t have to go and cough all over our lovely patrons.

6 p.m. My appetite has been suffering, but eventually I whip up one of my favorites: a bean medley, chickpea, celery, olive oil and feta salad.

8 p.m. As the sun sets and the self pity sinks in deeper, I throw a trench coat over my pajamas and scurry down to the store to get another favorite, a bottle of Te Henga Sauvignon Blanc. $19.45.

10 a.m. Another Americano and lemon water.

1 p.m. At this point in the week I am so sick of tea I never want to see it again. I’ve been trying to stave off whatever I have with honey/lemon/ginger tea and I’m over it. That was lunch, I guess.

8 p.m. Guilty pleasure time! I call in an order for Little Caesars Chicago Deep Dish Meat Treat pizza, an order of hot wings, and a ginger ale. Pure class and total nutrition. The good news is that while attempting to remain unseen, I happen to run into someone I’ve been chatting with on a dating app. Oh did I say good? I meant horrific. $39.77.

Recent findings suggest that 10 a.m. Americano. Lemon Water. I’m a creature of habit, ok?

12 p.m. Bananas, blueberries, leftover bean salad, ginger tea.

Sources indicate that 3 p.m. I’m at work early, because we have fresh menu items. At pre-shift, the chef makes one of each and we discuss and sample it. A prime rib chuck burger with scamorza and tomato bomba, lamb pizza with basil pesto, steak tartare, Atlantic cod and potato risotto, and mushroom and pea stuffed ravioli. Some call this “product knowledge.” I call it a free meal(s).

Recent findings suggest that 8:45 p.m. Despite all my newfound product knowledge, I still get hungry halfway through my shift. Chef makes me a bulgur, kale, and roasted beet salad with a 7oz flatiron steak. $22.

Sources indicate that 10:45 p.m. Shift done, head feeling like a block of ice, I sneak off to the market before heading home to grab a bottle of Squealing Pig Sauvignon Blanc. $22.

10 a.m. Pretty much right after I open my eyes I get a lovely text from a friend; “Wanna get breakfast?” She knows I’ve been sick and we haven’t caught up in a while. She is informed that I will be wearing my now-uniform of pajamas and trench coat.

Recent findings suggest that 11 a.m. Three eggs, toast, and bacon from a pub by my house. No culinary awards will be given out here but it did what it was supposed to do. The bill for both meals with coffee and a couple of spicy Bloody Caesars came to $50.

7 p.m. Another go-to when I’m feeling down or simply have the craving is to simmer some rice noodles in a broth and add miso paste. I stir in fresh chopped bok choy, green onions and a couple of cut-up hard boiled eggs. I think I’m gonna make it.

  • It has been revealed that tripadvisor has unwound a 2025 restructuring that combined its “things to do” and Viator experiences teams under one roof.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, photo Credit: Tripadvisor's Matt Goldberg was interviewed by Skift Research's Seth Borko at Skift Global Forum on September 19, 2024. Skift.

There's often a lot of hype about the strategic benefits in a restructuring. Tripadvisor admitted its November 2025 restructuring didn't work.

It has been revealed that tripadvisor has unwound a 2025 restructuring that combined its “things to do” and Viator experiences teams under one roof. The two businesses are back to separate teams, similar to how they were organized before the November 2025 changes, according to a source familiar with Tripadvisor’s operations.

In a recent development, under the new structure, Tripadvisor’s things to do business will have its own team. That business mainly generates leads for Viator, the company’s main experiences brand and the focus of its investment. Viator’s experiences operations will have a separate team.

In a November 4 internal email to employees, sent after an all-hands meeting at which outgoing CEO Matt Goldberg revealed a firm-wide restructuring, Tripadvisor President Kristen Dalton wrote: “Experiences will be singularly focused on the Viator and Bokun brands with a focus on growth.” Bokun is Tripadvisor’s back-end reservations technology business for experiences operators, not a con.

Ohio is known for a few familiar trademarks: itâs in the Midwest, for starters, and itâs home to the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame and endless cornfields. But the Buckeye State is so much more than crops, cows, and music memorabilia.Â.

Did you know the state also features Holmes County, one of the worldâs largest Amish communities; the Pro Football Hall of Fame; Cedar Point and its record-breaking roller coasters; and the birthplace of the famous Skyline Chili?

Aviation pioneers Wilbur and Orville Wright and astronaut Neil Armstrong, the first man to walk on the moon, were all born in the Buckeye State. Ohio saw the debut of the first professional baseball team, the Red Stockings, the first concrete road (paved in Bellefontaine in 1891), and the first electric traffic signal (installed in Cleveland in 1914). It also has the only state flag in the U.S. that isnât rectangular.

In a recent development, if that isnât enough to spark your interest, Superman was created in Cleveland in 1933! Yes, Clark Kent himself. And the light bulb, cash register, and zipper were all invented there.Â.

In recent years, âOhioâ has become an internet meme and slang term among Gen Z and Gen Alpha, used to describe something âweird, awkward, cringeworthy, or otherwise undesirable,â even âboring.â.

But Ohio is anything but dull and one-dimensional, from region to region and city to city. Speaking of cities, can you name the seven largest cities in the Buckeye State by population?

Industry observers note that how many of Ohioâs largest cities could you name? The first three probably came to mind faster than you could say âIâll have a chili cheese coney with chili cheese fries and a Cincinnati three-way,â but the rest were trickier, depending on where youâre from and how much you know about Ohio. Send this quiz to your friends to see how well they know the Buckeye State!Â.

In a recent development, according to National Geographic Kids, people have lived on the land we now call Ohio for at least 13,000 years. Archaeologists have discovered Ice Age tools and continue to uncover Native American artifacts from the Erie, Shawnee, and Kickapoo tribes.Â.

Ohio became a state in 1803, the same year the Louisiana Purchase treaty was signed, making it the 17th state admitted to the Union.

Why is it called Ohio? Well, we donât know for sure. Some believe the name comes from the Iroquois word âoyo,â meaning âthe great river,â perhaps the Ohio River.

Ohio has several distinct geographic regions: the northern Great Lakes Plains, the Till Plains, the Appalachian Plateau, and the Bluegrass Region, scattered throughout the state, all boasting natural beauty.Â.

According to recent reports, ohio is the birthplace of seven U.S. presidents (second only to Virginia, which claims eight native-born presidents): Ulysses S. Grant, Rutherford B. Hayes, James Garfield, Benjamin Harrison, William McKinley, William H. Taft, and Warren G. Harding.

#10. Breaking: The Best New Restaurants in America in 2026

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4517 w)
