Breaking: The Best New Restaurants in America in 2026

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The year’s top restaurant debuts give us infinite reasons to dine out right now.
  • These are the 15 fresh restaurants that best captured the year in dining.
  • It has been revealed that what we found remarkable: the quiet confidence of a chef who’s mastered Hungarian food in Pittsburgh; a fresh revamp of family-style Italian dining in Philadelphia grounded in the original restaurant’s 1950s roots; a cozy tribute to Southern cuisine in Denver that still manages to feel cool.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The year’s top restaurant debuts give us infinite reasons to dine out right now.

These are the 15 fresh restaurants that best captured the year in dining. Our team of editors and scouts traveled across the country, drawing on years of experience to build the 2026 winners list.

It has been revealed that what we found remarkable: the quiet confidence of a chef who’s mastered Hungarian food in Pittsburgh; a fresh revamp of family-style Italian dining in Philadelphia grounded in the original restaurant’s 1950s roots; a cozy tribute to Southern cuisine in Denver that still manages to feel cool. What they have in common: a sincere commitment to making diners feel at home. — Missy Frederick, editorial director.

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

Recent findings suggest that “You went to Kansas City for sushi?” I was asked more than once — with some derision — after returning from Missouri, so I can only imagine the uphill battle chef Peter Hoang faces at Akoya Omakase. Hoang isn’t easily daunted. He’s so committed to sourcing, he often personally drives to the airport to pick up the fish hand-selected by his two private buyers in Tokyo 26 hours after placing his order.

It has been revealed that at Akoya, the fish quality is unassailable; the rice seasoned with precision. But Hoang consistently finds ways to complement Akoya’s sashimi and nigiri with unexpected accents. Smoky juvenile king mackerel gets a hit of acid and sweetness from pineapple chutney. Truffle, notorious for being overwhelming on just about anything, manifests in pate form alongside dashi and kelp salt to highlight delicate hirame. The miso-butter-accented crab nigiri (a steal at $6) calls to mind decadently dipping crab legs in drawn butter. While affordable for omakase, $165 is still a commitment: Akoya diners have the option to test the waters with a la carte offerings and lunch specials in a warm and unpretentious restaurant. Befitting the Midwestern stereotype, the personable chefs, who chat freely with those seated across the bar, are eager to answer questions. Even tables in the dining room chime in.

Hoang, who worked in his father’s mid-2000s sushi restaurant before heading to bigger markets like Fresh York and Chicago, is excited to be part of his hometown’s emerging Japanese dining scene — one that’s increasingly drawing national attention thanks to ambitious restaurants like Anjin izakaya and promising newcomers like day-to-night Tian Tea House/Moon Bar. Kansas City just might develop a reputation for cuisine beyond barbecue. — MF.

Assuming newly introduced ownership of beloved, old restaurants can be a risk, but South Philly local Joey Baldino has the formula down: Keep the trappings, dial in the food. After taking over his family’s private Palizzi Social Club and retaining its members-only allure, Baldino bought Bomb Bomb Bar, which first opened in 1951, and reopened it last year. The bar’s lore precedes it: A rival business bombed it twice, immortalized by the large neon sign of two cartoonish bombs. Some reboots feel ironic, but not this one; the payphone by the door, the swordfish on the wall, and even the endearingly gruff servers feel like they’ve been there forever. It’s proof that classic Philly and modern culinary destination Philly can coexist.

In the front room, locals analyze Eagles games, and you might hear children playing in the street. In the back dining room, the procession of seafood here, priced at $65 per person, feels like a steal in this era of rising prices. The meat for the lobster Française has been removed from its shell, battered and fried, placed onto a buttery sauce, and then crowned with its shell once more. The crispy calamari gets enlivened with twangy cherry peppers. But it’s the overall dining experience that’s unbeatable: The restaurant hasn’t reinvented the wheel, but as the Beach Boys play and you sip a pepperoncini martini while watching your server pour hot fudge onto a sundae, you remember (perhaps while still wearing a bib) that complete novelty isn’t always necessary. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

In a recent development, cassis is significant in every sense. The nearly 200-seat dining room of the Milwaukee restaurant is an immaculately designed jewel box of gleaming tile, cozy banquettes, and antique mirrors, and even on a Wednesday night, it’s packed and roaring, with a towering, glowing bar at the center of the action. The latest project from Kyle and Meghan Knall, the couple behind nearby acclaimed bistro Birch, channels the conviviality and polish of a classic, old-world French brasserie while remaining distinctly Midwestern in spirit. It’s an all-day restaurant with both heart and panache.

Kyle Knall’s cooking roots itself in French tradition without feeling stodgy or like Parisian cosplay. Instead, it takes cues from his farm-to-table approach at Birch: Classical technique provides a framework for showing off Wisconsin ingredients with playfulness, vividness, and attention to detail. Oeuf mayo gets a jolt from intensely herbaceous, bright green aioli; ravioli Dauphiné pairs almost sugary-sweet summer corn with buttery Wisconsin-made Pleasant Ridge Reserve cheese; and an understated, frill-free but deeply umami foie gras eclair transforms one of French cuisine’s richest ingredients into an almost weightless bite.

At a moment when ambitious dining often means intimate tasting-menu counters and an air of exclusivity, Cassis makes a case that dinner can still feel like a real night out on the town. The cooking has an eagerness to please that succeeds. Within its walls, you’re offered an increasingly rare pleasure: a space where you’re invited to settle in, linger, order another bottle of wine, and maybe even have a friendly chat with the table next to you. Cassis could exist — and surely thrive — in New York or Las Vegas, but it’s more exciting in Milwaukee, where its scale and ambition feel like a vote of confidence in the city itself. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor, Eater.

In 2026, the Midwest has proven a formidable destination for dining, with restaurants from Cleveland to Milwaukee leaning into what makes the region’s food special. Creepies in Chicago embodies this movement: A nonsensical (if memorable) name belies a thoughtful restaurant destination from chefs David and Anna Posey. The refreshing space feels contemporary, but with cottage-esque touches — geometric patterns dot the furniture, cartoonish artwork shares space with kitchenware tchotchkes, and mini curtains hang from open shelving.

Chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski embeds French technique into dishes fiercely grounded in Chicago’s identity. Steamed mussels get kissed with classic Pernod and a fennel giardiniera that honors the city’s iconic Italian beef sandwiches. An Alsatian-leaning tarte flambe comes “tavern-style,” a nod to the square-cut pizza beloved by locals. Not every dish invokes the Great Lakes; the generous portion of gougeres may be Midwest-appropriate, but here the French classic takes a decadent turn as warm Brie seeps from the center of each choux pastry. A textbook roast chicken’s umami-laden sauce gains extra depth from liver; drag one of the restaurant’s hefty, yet impossibly crispy fries through its drippings for the best bite of the night. Save room for Anna Posey’s desserts: The savory soft-serve trend manifests as a baguette-infused concoction topped with chocolate and buttery breadcrumbs. In a year when a diner can grow weary that Everything’s a Bistro these days, Creepies proves some still offer delights and surprises. — MF.

According to recent reports, I’ve always felt a connection to Cuban cuisine, having visited the island country in my youth and eaten many pan con lechons from LA’s Porto’s Bakery in iconic Glendale. But a July meal at Emelina, which snagged a Michelin star months after opening for its ambitious, $275 Cuban tasting menu, revealed me the country’s cooking in an entirely latest context.

Recent findings suggest that I wasn’t the only one to find it a revelation. Several older Cubans fortunate enough to nab a reservation got emotional toward the end of the meal, moved to tears as they told me they’d never had Cuban food like this before.

According to recent reports, located in tony West Palm Beach, this striking restaurant from chefs Osmel González and Camila Salazar draws inspiration from the former’s family history and upbringing in Cuba. After working together at world-class restaurants like Disfrutar in Spain and SingleThread in California, they partnered with Alvaro Perez-Miranda to achieve their vision. Employing lush ingredients sourced from South Florida farms in Redland and Lake Worth, the meal starts with a tender knob of fried flounder topped with caviar — a winking nod to traditional pan con minuta, a fried fish sandwich slathered with tartar sauce. A mid-course of pristine tropical fruits including mamey, lychee, and mango, arranged over creamy ricotta and dotted with Benton’s country ham, conjures a bounty one might linger over on a Cuban beach. Rabo encendido, or braised oxtail with Koshihikari rice, takes the homestyle guisado to latest heights.

It has been revealed that cuba has a long history of home restaurants called paladares, serving personalized versions of staple dishes like arroz con pollo. Emelina represents that same opportunity to delight and enlighten, casting attention on a cuisine and culture that could have been. In balmy West Palm Beach, it thrives. — Matthew Kang, correspondent.

The winding walkway into Maroon is a portal into a fresh dimension, a leap from the beeps and bloops of the casino floor at the Sahara Las Vegas into a thrumming dining room, dimly lit and streaked with red-orange accents. Chef Kwame Onwuachi, who most recently earned acclaim at Tatiana in New York City and Dōgon in Washington, D.C., has become a beacon of African diasporic dishes in the middle of the Mojave Desert.

Recent findings suggest that onwuachi is building something approachable yet grounded in technique. The name Maroon comes from 17th- and 18th-century enslaved people who escaped and established mountain communities in Jamaica; the kitchen centers African and Caribbean flavors rooted in their foodways. Consider the artful array of bluefin tuna belly chunks, hamachi, and braised octopus, swimming in a tangy broth pool and best enjoyed spooned onto fried saltine crackers, that gets an intense but brief spice hit from Scotch bonnet peppers. Luxurious, palm-sized oxtail patties and jerk mushroom earn a dash of caviar and grated truffle, a maximalist garnish on the typically humble dish. Grilled butterflied shrimp brushed with achiote sofrito recall pescado zarandeado, while sweet white grape chow chow brings a puckery kick. The blackened jerk chicken, its juiciness sealed in with a crust of aromatic spices, might be the finest in the U.S.; oxtail fried rice could moonlight as Caribbean bibimbap, with saucy deboned beef and fork-tender stewed chicken on an assemblage of julienned peppers and peas. Yes, there is steak, but go for the seared, bone-in pork chop instead for its sweet glaze.

It has been revealed that maroon engages you with sensory brilliance and familiar yet indelible flavors, like a catchy song that gets better with each listen. In a different city, it might feel overwrought, but here in Las Vegas, it matches the city’s frenetic energy and lands like a satisfying opus. — MK.

Maydan Market opened in 2025 as a collaborative restaurant space and marketplace home to a few different Los Angeles-born businesses; in essence, it functions as one super-incubator for some of the best food you can find in the city. Diners bounce around to try a pozole flight and pescadillas (sofrito-fried fish nested in supple blue corn tortillas) at Maléna, from the family behind the beloved Tamales Elena; a crisp, UFO-sized, asiento-painted tlayuda from Lugya’h, from Los Angeles legend Poncho’s Tlayudas; and chile-sauce-slicked gai tod from Golden Mountain Chicken (formerly Yhing Yhang), from the intrepid team behind Thai restaurant Holy Basil. They will certainly stop to perch at the rotating Club 104 stall, which has hosted Black-owned businesses such as Melnificent Wingz and Caribbean diasporic pop-up Rubie, as well as Palestinian home restaurant Mid East Eats. On their way out, they may circle the storefront simply named Sook to eye wines, spices, and woven goods sourced from the Levant.

This is not to mention the market’s anchor restaurants: the Lebanese-influenced Maydan and Compass Rose, respectable D.C. transplants from prolific restaurateur Rose Previte, who, alongside her team, curated the market with the knockout lineup of Indigenous vendors. Maydan Market feels boldly like one whole; people rarely come for a single hyped stall. The point, in effect, is the crawl. In a year marked by ongoing, unrelenting, nationwide ICE raids targeting Black and brown immigrants, the fact that the market centers Indigenous Mexican-owned businesses, allowing their owners the space and sovereignty to reach a wider stage and audience, speaks loudly. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Take the former location of Portland’s — if not North America’s — most famous Northern Thai restaurant, combine it with the city’s most prolific and highly decorated Thai chef and restaurateur in Akkapong “Earl” Ninsom, and pepper in an elite local bar manager — co-owner Eric Nelson. Mix it all together, and you get OK Chicken & Khao Soi. Those familiar with its predecessor, Pok Pok, will find the space uncannily similar: a covered patio and downstairs service at a small bar, upstairs seating at oilcloth-wrapped tables. Now customers order on paper tabs. It’s casual and intimate, with just the right level of noise to feel like you stumbled into a really good dinner party.

OK Chicken’s menu leans into the flavors of Chiang Mai, starting with crispy chicken wings and two styles of khao soi — one with chicken and another richly prepared with beef. Plates of smoky nam prik makheua (eggplant dip) come with crisp and waxy long beans, green cabbage leaves, and cucumber. A memorable dish of yum moo yang — tender grilled pork shoulder tossed with snappish chunks of celery stalk and leaves as well as sliced onion — relaxes in a funky fish sauce with Thai chiles that sneakily build in your system until your lips hum. An herbal tea slushie refreshes even when mixed with a shot of infused Scotch. Close the meal with longan sticky rice speckled with perilla seeds, showered with crispy coconut and bathed in salted coconut milk that balances the sweetness of the pale lychee fruit and tangy mango ice cream on top. Each bite or sip at OK Chicken is surprising and pleasurable in equal measure. — Brenna Houck, dining editorial manager.

In kitchens across the country, chefs have been happily marrying Japanese and Mexican foodways: Both cuisines have a reverence for local grains, honor highly specific seafood preparations, and play on savory, acidic flavors. Ramen Del Barrio blossomed from this shared cultural language — a Japanese Mexican izakaya centering ramen.

Industry observers note that chef and owner Chris Krinsky deftly laces together these threads for dishes such as creamy carnitas tonkotsu with two types of pork, confit buche and belly, as well as a chewy tangle of fresh noodles — made in partnership with Austin chef Gary Wu — using flour from a local mill. A honeycomb tripe and hominy-studded pozole tonkotsu comes rojo- or verde-style, while the mole tsukemen gets paired with thick whole wheat noodles and carnitas for dipping into rich, hearty mole. Tuna tostada, served on top of a sheet of origami paper, packs a zesty punch thanks to a dried shrimp and morita chile aioli, chicharrones furikake, eel sauce, and salsa macha. The yaki-tacos — hefty yakitori skewers served on top of corn tortillas — use smoky pulpo and vegetarian-friendly mushrooms accented with pepitas.

It has been revealed that this isn’t fusion for fusion’s sake. Krinsky was born in Maine, grew up in Mexico, and worked at Japanese restaurants throughout most of his career. He started his ramen journey cooking out of his garage and then opened a food court stand, for which he won an Eater Award in 2023. Somehow, his menu tastes better now that he has his own dedicated space where he hand-layered wood panels along the wall and lined the ceiling with sushi mats. A small television in the dining room blasts Spanish-dubbed anime. Ramen Del Barrio 2.0 feels wholly like a loving expression of his culinary fascinations and his commitment to honoring both traditions. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York.

In a recent development, in an unmarked space in San Francisco’s Nob Hill, chef Patrick Gabon and partner Celine Wuu quietly rewrote the playbook on fine dining with Restaurant Naides. Filipino food has not historically held a footing in the Bay Area’s higher-end echelons, but Naides’s dishes make a powerful claim that the cuisine deserves its place there. Gabon deploys the sour, salty, and sweet flavors of the Philippines with subtle tenacity: The saline funk of bagoong, or fermented salted shrimp, takes on upcoming dimension in Gabon’s hands, where the condiment gets mellowed into a creamy sauce that acts as foil to tender slices of chayote, crisp duck cracklings, and the burst of caviar. His approach to the mouth-puckering sourness of sinigang invigorates the Philippines’ national dish by pouring dry-aged beef broth over meticulously sliced abalone and scallions. These plates manage to retain the soul of the food but in new forms; they don’t placate the audience, asking them instead to reconsider their fundamental notions of fine dining and how Filipino food presented in this way may upend them.

In a recent development, wuu’s beverage program has become a force of its own. It’s not often that a nonalcoholic pairing manages to outshine a traditional wine program, but Wuu keenly matches the bold flavors of each dish. A drink mixing the flavors of green mango with rooibos and habañero cordial complements the salty punch of bagoong at one turn, while coconut water, osmanthus, and rose vinegar offer a gentle start with the opening snacks, composed of Gabon’s takes on lumpia, okoy, and puto. “As you age and you grow, you tend to go deeper in your roots: ‘How can I make something so traditional the best it can be?’” Wuu told me earlier this year. Naides has answered that question with every meal since. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF.

It has been revealed that it’s tricky to pin down what exactly Rougarou is. It’s a restaurant, certainly, serving modern Southern food in the historic Five Points neighborhood in Denver. It also has a ripping bar program, late-night hours, live music on the patio, and a casual roguish charm. Inside an understated brick building on a flyby street, the dining room is full of personality, dim and moody, all hard surfaces that bounce around the fun clatter of spirited groups throughout the dinner hour.

Recent findings suggest that the menu conveys the right balance of accessibility and intrigue: The ubiquitous tomato stone fruit salad gets a curry-inflected jolt of vinaigrette and a crunch of coconut benne granola. Charred zucchini is doused in smoked cheddar sauce and scattered with bits of country ham. Fried catfish sits on a pond of fermented hot and sour sauce, with pickled chiles that lash the tongue at first and Sichuan peppercorns that leave you gently tingling. And the signature Chicken on a Stick is a lovingly updated homage to a legendary gas station restaurant in Oxford, Mississippi.

Industry observers note that while the food feels approachable, the cocktails are high-concept and assertive, leaning on tropical ingredients but pushing for wilder edges, like green banana, oversteeped oolong, and Haitian clairin, pungent and unctuous with fusel oils. A second visit, late at night, revealed a laid-back restaurant-industry hangout at the bar instead of the celebratory din I found earlier. Much like its namesake monster, Rougarou can shape-shift to host a group dinner, a date night, a jam session, or a beguiling nightcap. It’s the kind of restaurant that invites returns, and a great fit for this moment in restaurant culture. — Ben Mesirow, travel editor.

Recent findings suggest that D.C. hospitality veterans Jon Sybert and Jill Tyler took a risk when they converted Adams Morgan’s Michelin-starred favorite Tail Up Goat into Rye Bunny, a restaurant that straddles the line between upscale and casual. Appetizers start at $15 and entree prices go up to $40, and instead of table service, diners line up to order at a counter. In the end, both the owners and D.C. diners have seen a payoff. Sybert’s dishes are inventive yet comforting, with Aleppo honey-covered fried chicken served alongside delicately stacked anchovy and quince jam toasts built on thin slices of milk bread. Everything is still seasonal and sourced from nearby farms, but those high-grade ingredients are easier to afford now that the restaurant has been able to cut down on the number of staff by 20 percent. While D.C. diners are not crazy about queuing, the nightly line out the door has sustained for more than six months and become an unexpected way to meet neighbors. A server brings over a drink menu as you wait, so you can catch up with friends and sip on a Slovenian orange wine before you sit down.

Recent findings suggest that rye Bunny encompasses the simple joy of a neighborhood restaurant that’s an equally excellent destination for a weekday date night or a special occasion, and it represents a larger shift in our dining landscape that might save these mid-price-range restaurants as margins get thinner. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

When So. Fox opened in Atlanta’s Virginia-Highland neighborhood in July, chef Myles Moody and sommelier Rachael Pack had an instant hit, bringing newly introduced energy to that pocket of the city. But a successful restaurant often belies monumental effort behind the scenes. So. Fox’s signature dish — a whole roasted chicken — is only available to five lucky tables per night and regularly sells out before the second seating. Much like a great restaurant takes time to build, the simple bird takes days for its mustard brine to infuse, and the result is stunning: a glistening interior and exquisitely crispy skin.

According to recent reports, so. Fox commands an insatiable demand for a table topped with that prized poultry, herby rabbit dumplings, and Carolina Gold rice. Snagging a spot at the welcoming bar or at the curved, floating table near the entry, which helps capture overflow crowds, is equally competitive. The space that formerly housed a burger joint (and before that, an auto repair shop) has been transformed into a bright, perennially packed dining room with grand windows, offering an optimal view of North Highland Avenue.

Short for Southern Fox, an American indigenous grape varietal, So. Fox showcases Pack’s longtime knowledge of natural, low-intervention, biodynamic, and Old World producers, many of whom she knows personally. Pack and Atlanta-born Moody first met while working at New York’s Michelin-starred Aska, and returned south to open Kinship Butcher & Sundry in 2021, which resides next door. This isn’t just farm-to-table; it’s produce from their own Ormewood Park farm, highlighted in grilled beef with Vidalia onions and braised leeks, and at the end of summer, in sugar snap peas with chives and farmer cheese.

It’s seasonal Southern fare that feels current and relevant, with a refreshingly casual approach — and people can’t help but show up for it. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater LA.

Somssi, from Ahris Kim and chef Daniel Gronert, is one of the clearest examples in Newly introduced York of a restaurant that goes all-in on personal history, rather than focusing on the broader food culture of any one country or a region.

Korea-born Kim, who ran operations at Atomix, lived in Indonesia and the Philippines before moving to Wisconsin with her family. Gronert, who has German roots and spent time as a pitmaster in South Carolina, cooked across restaurants in Atomix’s parent company. Those influences show up in dishes like the caviar-crowned Potato Potato Potato, a crispy-soft tater tot simulacrum nested on miso hollandaise; ox tongue grilled and glazed with tare, a kaleidoscope of textures; and pork schnitzel presented like shrimp toast (it works).

With the team’s fine dining pedigree, Somssi sets a high bar for hospitality, yet it’s still casual: The room is designed to feel like a home, and the menu nods to places Kim and Gronert have lived.

According to recent reports, the bar extends that expertise. Christian Gray’s cocktails include well-made minis, which the bartenders are game to explain to curious drinkers. Sommelier (and Punch contributor) Jenny Eagleton’s list of wines and sakes leans toward lesser-known areas. The duo and their staff reward handing your night over to them, whether you’re there with a group or alone with a Kindle.

Recent findings suggest that personal touches carry through the space in gloriously analog fashion. Lace curtains on the door spell out the restaurant’s name in embroidery, and handprints line the bathroom wall, left by the broader constellation of people who helped build Somssi into the singular restaurant it is today. — NC.

In a recent development, sunday is a very good night to be at Titusz. That’s Schnitzel Sonntag — when the Pittsburgh restaurant, clad in warm wood and gem-toned ceramic tile, offers an irresistible special at an even more irresistible price: a 4-ounce veal cutlet, breaded and fried in lard, for $13. The golden brown slab comes with a single lemon cheek on the plate and nothing else. It takes confidence to serve a dish so simply: Chef and owner Csilla Thackray gained hers in some of the city’s top restaurant kitchens. She named Titusz after her great-grandfather, and his portrait hangs by the first-floor bar. Her own name comes from her Budapest-born grandmother, who raised the chef on her cooking.

Call it grandmacore if you want to peg Titusz to a national trend, but the menu is modern, Austrian, Hungarian, and distinctly Thackray’s. Here, meggyleves, the Magyar sour-cherry soup, gets an electrifying swirl of paprika oil. The chef has made charring an art: You will want to pick up the bowl and drink every drop of charred leek and sauerkraut broth beneath her buoyant kaspressknödel (cheese dumplings). The Maillard reaction pays off again in the savory brown butter drizzled over a dessert of aranygaluska (think walnut monkey bread), served warm on a puddle of peach creme anglaise. Thackray’s husband — Sean Rosenkrans, another veteran of Pittsburgh’s restaurant scene — has built a stunning list of wines from Central Europe, as well as cocktails fluent in that idiom — a slug of herbal Unicum here, a toasty hint of caraway there. Everything makes profound and reassuring sense together. The decision to spend money at a restaurant might feel fraught right now; the choices at Titusz never do. — Beth Kracklauer, dining editorial manager.

The Areni-1 Cave Shoe in Yerevan, Armenia

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This leather shoe was discovered in Areni 1 cave during excavations in 2008.
  • Made from a single piece of cowhide leather, and still with its leather laces it has been measured as corresponding to a modern US size 7 / EU size 37 / UK size 6.
  • Researchers have managed to date it back to 3600-3500 BC based on the radiocarbon dating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This leather shoe was discovered in Areni 1 cave during excavations in 2008.

Made from a single piece of cowhide leather, and still with its leather laces it has been measured as corresponding to a modern US size 7 / EU size 37 / UK size 6. It is stuffed with grass to either maintain its shape or keep the foot warm. It is unknown at this stage whether it was a man or woman's shoe.

Researchers have managed to date it back to 3600-3500 BC based on the radiocarbon dating.

The shoe managed to survive in near-perfect condition because of the cool, dry cave environment which was sealed off by several layers of sheep dung. The shoe was found upside down at the base of a shallow, rounded, and plastered pit, beneath an overturned broken Chalcolithic ceramic bowl.

The museum can be accessed for a fee.

The shoe is one of the earliest exhibits on display.

Recent findings suggest that this is only the third nationwide ground stop in 25 years. The last one, during a 2023 system outage, lasted about two hours.

The Federal Aviation Administration ended a nationwide ground stop Friday night more than four hours after a communication issue affected the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, the high-altitude air traffic control facilities that manage flights between airports.

According to recent reports, the ground stop was lifted at around 8:15 p.m. ET, but disruptions are expected to linger into the weekend.

In a recent development, as of Saturday morning, there were more than 4,000 flight cancellations, according to FlightAware. Airlines canceled over 9,000 flights on Friday.

During a televised briefing Friday night, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin noted there was no indication of a cyberattack.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted at 3:36 p.m. ET the FAA started "experiencing instability" at radar and communication at air traffic control centers and TRACONs (Terminal Radar Approach Controls). He said 3,500 planes were in the air at the time.

It has been revealed that america is synonymous with fast food: burgers, fries, Coney dogs, chicken tenders; you name it! Â But it hasn't always been like this.Â.

According to recent reports, according to Taste of Home, the first fast-food chain restaurant in the United States was A&W, which popped up in 1919. The chain, with its famous Root Beer float and hamburger family, remained relevant into the 1970s, when its brick-and-mortar locations actually outnumbered McDonald's.

White Castle was established in 1921, followed by a series of chains in the 1940s.

In a recent development, adam Chandler, author of Drive-Thru Dreams, noted that the American fast-food boom coincided with the development of the U.S. highway system in the 1950s and '60s.

Recent findings suggest that "America started driving more than ever before, and we rearranged our cities based on car travel, for better or worse. And it was a natural business response to the American on-the-go kind of lifestyle," he explained to Smithsonian Magazine.

Still, the 1940s had several popular fast-food spots where customers could grab a quick, cheap meal: A&W and White Castle, along with new arrivals like Dairy Queen (1940), Dunkin' Donuts (1948), and In-N-Out Burger (1948).

Industry observers note that speedy, on-the-go service wasn't the only reason fast-food restaurants thrived in the U.S. Chandler pointed out that these establishments are unique in the way they bring people together.

Sources indicate that "You can go into a McDonaldâs, you can go into a Taco Bell, and you will see literally every demographic group there. Old, young, all races, all ages, all economic backgrounds, kind of sharing a meal. There arenât a lot of places that offer that.".

Recent findings suggest that it's no secret that fast-food restaurants might not serve the most nutritious meals, but they're quick, easy, and cheap. Sometimes, that's all people are looking for, especially when they're traveling or in a time crunch.

#6. Fugitive imagination

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3320 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Aeon ↗ Open Full Page

Fugitive imagination

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1986, I was 19 and behind bars in a small prison on the border between Iran and Pakistan.
  • Recent findings suggest that yet we all shared one thing.
  • Industry observers note that that prison experience was perhaps one reason I became a scholar of borders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1986, I was 19 and behind bars in a small prison on the border between Iran and Pakistan. I had been arrested while attempting to cross the border irregularly into Pakistan. Everyone I met in that prison had been detained in connection with the border. It was a small space, the cells overcrowded and unsanitary, but it held an extraordinary diversity of people: local smugglers, large-scale drug-traffickers, undocumented migrant workers, and refugees; Iranians, Afghans, Pakistanis, as well as Baluch men whose communities had crossed these lands freely for generations but who were now being punished for violating the territorial order of the nation-state. Multiple languages were spoken at once. Different histories, geographies and ways of inhabiting the world converged within the same confined space.

Recent findings suggest that yet we all shared one thing. We had refused, for different reasons, to respect the border. The state saw us through a single imaginary: as criminals, trespassers or illegal bodies to be contained. We, however, were animated by different imaginations. Each of us had imagined a life that exceeded the border and acted upon that imagination. In that sense, the prison did not simply contain border-crossers; it brought together people whose aspirations had collided with the territorial imaginary of the nation-state.

Industry observers note that that prison experience was perhaps one reason I became a scholar of borders. It remains, even today, the most crucial school of border studies I have ever attended. The conversations in the cells and during brief moments in the prison yard revolved around borders; how they operated, how they were enforced and, above all, how they might be circumvented. The prison became an unlikely site of knowledge-production: not simply the sharing of survival strategies but the enactment of an imagination that paid no heed to prison walls or state borders.

Many years later, in a prison north of Stockholm, I interviewed a human smuggler who told me he saw himself as an architect: ‘I design a journey, like an architect designs a building,’ he said. The comparison stayed with me. Architects imagine and design structures that do not yet exist. Their work begins with the capacity to visualise what is not yet visible. In a similar way, smugglers design border crossings that, from the perspective of the state, would be impossible. A smuggler’s work consists of imagining routes where borders appear closed, creating connections where states impose separation, and envisioning possibilities for mobility when people are immobilised by borders. A smuggler speculates on possibilities in seemingly impossible situations. Seen this way, the smuggler’s ‘architecture’ is an enactment of an imagination that refuses the state imaginary expressed through borders.

The parallels between human smuggling and architecture helped me understand the relationship between imagination, fugitivity and knowledge-production. While fugitivity and imagination are oriented toward the future, toward not-yet-realised possibilities, state power often relies on backward-looking imaginaries grounded in myths of shared blood, origin and belonging. States are hostile to this relationship because it exposes borders as political constructions that can be reimagined, negotiated and crossed. Like capitalism, the nation-state depends upon such imaginaries to stabilise its claims to totality, making it difficult to imagine a world beyond capitalism and the nation-state system.

Precisely because imagination opens the possibility of other worlds, states often regard it as a threat.

All around us, across the world, people are being confined, displaced, silenced and rendered disposable, in service of imaginaries that seek to define the limits of life, mobility and freedom. We live in a conjunctural moment shaped by the convergence of two dark forces: borderless wars that destroy lives, produce death and generate displacement, and endless borders that deny mobility to those seeking survival. Together, they produce fugitive lives and fugitive bodies. But they also produce fugitive imagination, the irreducible capacity to envision and enact life beyond the worlds that seek to contain it.

Recent findings suggest that philosophers often define imagination as the capacity to hold present in the mind what is absent from sensory perception. It is also the capacity to envision alternative ways of organising social reality. Precisely because imagination opens the possibility of other worlds, states often regard it as a threat. The state-centric imaginary presents history as coherent, and intact through symbols, narratives and rituals. The capacity to disrupt the hegemony of state imaginaries is therefore criminalised, suppressed and persecuted. In this sense, fugitivity is inseparable from imagination.

In a recent development, A fugitive is someone fleeing harsh institutions and conditions. The fugitive is an outlaw: a person hiding from a hostile law. Historically, the term referred to enslaved people’s resistance to slavery, its dehumanising logic, and the political economy built upon the extraction of uncompensated labour to maximise profits from cash crops like cotton, tobacco and sugar. Fugitivity was a response to captivity and, as such, an act of liberation, not only from the brutal material conditions of enslavement, but also from the imposed image of the enslaved subject produced by racist ideology. Fugitivity is a way of escaping and a way of knowing.

When Frederick Douglass, one of the most crucial figures in the 19th-century struggle for African American freedom and civil rights, began learning to read, his enslaver Hugh Auld forbade it, declaring that, if Douglass learned to read, ‘there would be no keeping him’. Once capable of reading, Auld argued, Douglass would inevitably desire to write, and ‘this accomplished, he will be running away with himself.’.

Industry observers note that this phrase is striking. It suggests a distinction between the enslaved person and the enslaved body. To ‘run away with oneself’ is not simply to flee physically; it is to reclaim one’s imagination and humanity. Under slavery, where Black bodies were turned into capital, fugitivity was criminalised as theft. The fugitive was pursued by law because they were perceived to have stolen property from their enslaver: their own body. In reality, they were reclaiming what had first been stolen from them. If the captivity of the body depends upon the captivity of the mind, then the emancipation of consciousness becomes a precondition for bodily liberation. Such emancipation engenders latest subjectivities and creates the conditions for imagining what previously appeared impossible: life beyond chains, borders and confinement. Auld’s anxiety over Douglass’s literacy reflected precisely this logic. His fear was not simply the loss of labour, but the emergence of a subject who would not obey the racial imaginary; ‘he will be running away with himself.’.

Literacy was inseparable from emancipation, whereas pedagogy became fugitive.

The condition of fugitivity emerged from a radical imagination capable of envisioning existence beyond oppression. As a refusal of captivity, it entailed an inner transformation – a reorientation of consciousness that makes escape conceivable in the first place. This is the transformative power of imagination: it enables subjects to perceive possibilities beyond the limits imposed by domination. As Frantz Fanon reminds us in The Wretched of the Earth (1961), resistance opens a path toward liberation through a radical transformation of consciousness. Fugitivity is therefore a refusal to be objectified, categorised and reduced to the singular identities imposed by colonial imaginaries. The passage from subjection to freedom, from a colonial imaginary to a fugitive imagination, is thus a process of self-actualisation and the cultivation of what might be called a consciousness of refusal.

It has been revealed that despite prohibition and danger, Douglass pursued literacy covertly. Reading and writing eventually enabled him to forge passes for himself and others and to flee bondage. Literacy was thus inseparable from emancipation, whereas pedagogy became fugitive in two senses: first, because it was concerned with experiences of flight, concealment and resistance; and, second, because it was itself practised under conditions of flight and opacity.

Recent findings suggest that knowing the emancipatory power of education, many enslaved people continued to learn despite violent restrictions and anti-literacy laws. In Fugitive Pedagogy: Carter G Woodson and the Art of Black Teaching (2021), the historian Jarvis Givens traces the history of criminalised Black education in the United States, documenting the struggles of Black educators and students against centuries of anti-literacy laws and racist policing. The struggle surrounding Black education did not end with slavery, continuing instead through the era of racial segregation under Jim Crow and into the present. Contemporary attacks on Black studies and critical race theory in the US are among the latest examples of hostility toward forms of knowledge that expose structures of racial subordination.

In recent years, operations by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to arrest undocumented migrants have often been conducted near schools, where parents drop off and pick up their children. Such practices have deterred many parents from sending their children to school for fear of detention and deportation. One of the consequences of these enforcement strategies is that they undermine access to education and disrupt the pedagogical conditions. A study of five California school districts found a 22 per cent increase in daily student absences following ICE raids conducted in early 2025.

Recent findings suggest that the situation is not much different in Europe. Universities are increasingly shaped by hostile political climates in which curricula are regulated, funding is reduced, and critical fields of enquiry are delegitimised. In such contexts, critical knowledge itself becomes fugitive. For example, Sweden recently proposed a controversial law requiring state employees, including teachers and university professors, to report undocumented migrants to the police; following protests, the law was amended to exclude teachers and doctors, but tax officers and insurance agents must still ‘snitch’ on the undocumented.

Across different historical periods and geographical contexts, we see attempts to control or criminalise education in order to reproduce the state imaginary and suppress any stirrings of a fugitive imagination.

Recent findings suggest that palestine offers a striking example of the relationship between imagination, knowledge and fugitivity. Palestinian resistance is sustained by a fugitive imagination of freedom beyond colonial domination. Israel’s continued imposition of its colonial imaginary through occupation, genocide and scholasticide therefore targets not only Palestinian bodies and institutions but also the spaces in which alternative futures are imagined. (‘Scholasticide’ describes the systematic destruction of educational institutions and schools in Palestine by Israel.) This is why schools, universities and cultural institutions have repeatedly become targets of repression.

Since the start of the recent genocide in Gaza, more than 95 per cent of schools have been damaged or destroyed, disrupting the education of nearly 700,000 students. All 19 of Gaza’s recognised higher education institutions, including 12 universities, have been destroyed, and approximately 100 university professors have been killed. Yet attacks on Palestinian education did not begin with the current war.

Called ‘cells of illegal education’ by the Israeli authorities, underground schools were frequently raided.

Systematic destruction of educational infrastructures has been part of the war against Palestine since the early 1970s when the first higher education institutions emerged. Birzeit University, one of the most key centres of Palestinian intellectual life, was repeatedly closed by Israeli authorities. Between 1973 and 1992, the university was shut down 15 times, including a closure of almost four and a half years during the First Intifada. Starting in 1987, this period saw Palestinian education literally criminalised; repression only intensified. All six universities, 13 colleges and approximately 1,200 schools were closed.

Yet the suppression of formal education also generated fugitive pedagogical practices. As schools and universities were closed, teaching moved into homes, churches and mosques. Called ‘cells of illegal education’ by the Israeli authorities, these underground schools were frequently raided. ‘Soldiers would throw teargas grenades into the room to force all the students out, then split up so one group could arrest those who fled while the other would destroy science equipment or photocopiers and, later on, computers,’ writes Gabi Baramki in Peaceful Resistance: Building a Palestinian University Under Occupation (2009). Students escaped through windows or across roofs. Teachers and students who got arrested for organising and attending ‘cells of illegal education’ were charged with a ‘public order offence’.

Industry observers note that the Palestinian case demonstrates that education is never merely about knowledge. It is also a site of political struggle because it cultivates the fugitive imagination, the capacity to envision freedom beyond the colonial imaginaries that sustain occupation.

Since the Taliban regained control of Afghanistan in August 2021, they have systematically restricted the rights and freedoms of women and girls. One of their earliest targets was female education. In March 2022, the Taliban banned girls and women from attending secondary schools and universities. According to UNESCO, by August 2025 nearly 2.2 million Afghan girls were barred from education beyond the primary level.

Recent findings suggest that the criminalisation of female education has, however, generated resistance. Across Afghanistan, underground educational initiatives have emerged to challenge these restrictions. In parts of Kabul, local networks have organised clandestine schools hidden from the authorities. Living rooms, basements and private halls have been transformed into classrooms where small groups of girls continue to learn, despite the risks involved. If fugitivity in relation to education was historically shaped by race in the US, in Afghanistan it is profoundly shaped by gender. The struggle over women’s education is about regulation of who may know and imagine otherwise. What the Taliban fear is not women’s education but the fugitive imagination it cultivates. The Taliban know that literacy transforms consciousness. It enables women to refuse the patriarchal imaginary and to imagine lives beyond the confines it imposes.

According to recent reports, the Taliban’s fear echoes Auld’s reaction to Douglass’s literacy. Auld warned that if an enslaved person learned to read, ‘he would at once become unmanageable’. The Taliban’s concern follows the same logic: a woman who acquires knowledge runs away with herself.

The history of fugitivity is deeply entangled with the history of modernity itself, a modernity grounded in racial capitalism and constituted through colonialism and the nation-state system. This connection can be seen in the continuity between enslaved people fleeing plantations and refugees crossing contemporary state borders – indeed, the words ‘refugee’ and ‘fugitive’ share the same etymological root in the Latin fugere, meaning ‘to flee’. So, it makes sense that Moria Camp on the Greek island of Lesvos, once the largest and most notorious refugee camp in Europe, offers another insight into how fugitivity and imagination are interlinked.

Set up in January 2013, the camp’s harsh militarised regulation, spatial design and material conditions produced what might be called a camp imaginary, an expression of Europe’s border regime and its political desires, positioning refugees as unwanted, unfree and disposable subjects. Yet Moria was also a site where refugees created alternative spaces of learning, artistic expression and collective care. Through education, music, art and everyday acts of mutual support, they generated conditions that made survival possible. As Yannis Hamilakis demonstrated in his archaeological study of Moria, refugees created spaces for imagining precisely what the camp sought to render impossible: life beyond its spatial and political boundaries. In this sense, the camp was not only a space of confinement but also a site of fugitive imagination.

The final act of this fugitivity came in 2020: after years of overcrowding and unsafe conditions, the camp burned down. Yet the most enduring expression of fugitive imagination was not the end of the camp itself but the lives that emerged from it. Many former residents became filmmakers, musicians, poets, researchers and activists, demonstrating that, while the camp sought to contain people physically, it could not extinguish their capacity to imagine and create otherwise.

A fugitive imagination emerges through the practical and intellectual labour of navigating violence.

Survival under conditions of violence requires an intimate knowledge of violence – its logics, structures and repetitions. Such knowledge is necessary not only to endure violence but also to resist the imaginaries that sustain it. Drawing upon the idea of ‘borderland thinking’ – a concept originating from the Chicana scholar and poet Gloria Anzaldúa, which centres knowledge produced through the lived experience of physical and cultural borders – I think of fugitive imagination as a form of situated knowledge produced by people who must survive systems of capture, confinement and bordering. Anzaldúa, who grew up in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas, on the US-Mexico border, conceptualised the borderlands as a space of imagination through what she called la facultad:.

For people of the borderlands, la facultad is both a method of knowledge-production and a vital survival skill; it emerges not despite conditions of vulnerability and violence but through them. In the same manner, a fugitive imagination emerges through the practical and intellectual labour of navigating violence, even as it envisions possibilities beyond it.

It has been revealed that to gain access to imagination, to learn how to cultivate and enact it, is to break with the imaginaries that make every future appear the same. It is to create, within the present, the conditions for something that does not yet exist. Politics, then, is not only a struggle over power. It is also a struggle over images, imaginaries and imagination itself. It is a battle over what can be thought, what can be desired, and what can still be made possible.

In a recent development, earlier this year, I received a WhatsApp call from a childhood friend. We had grown up together in a small village in southwestern Iran, and it was the first call I had received from Iran in more than three months. The latest dreadful period had begun in December 2025 with the violent suppression of public protests; initially sparked by frustration over an economic crisis, they’d soon developed into a broad uprising. The Iranian state’s response was brutal. Thousands of people were killed and many more arrested. The state had cut off not only internet access but also much of the country’s telecommunications infrastructure. Iranians were still in shock from the militarised crackdown when an intense US-Israel war with Iran began on the last day of February 2026, bringing even more death and silence.

According to recent reports, when my friend’s name appeared on my screen, I hesitated before answering. I felt ashamed: I did not know how to speak to someone who had lived through so much violence while I remained safe. I called him back later that day, after collecting myself. The connection was poor and our conversation fragmented: a word here, a phrase there, only occasionally a complete sentence. But I was surprised – unsettled, in fact – by what I was able to piece together. Spring, I heard him say, had brought abundant rain. Alongside bombs and bullets, rain had fallen, more than in previous years. What arrived through his fragmented voice was not words but imagination.

In a recent development, I imagined the mountains saturated with water, the springs running full, the wheat fields nourished and waiting to be harvested. Even as US bombs materialised a colonial imaginary that sought to reorder the world according to imperial logics of domination, people continued to imagine rain, harvests, seasons. To look toward the sky and see rain falling alongside bombs was a refusal of the imperial imaginary – an imagination of life, despite everything, an imagination that cannot be killed, bombed, stolen or abducted, and from which the seeds of an alternative future might emerge.

Recent findings suggest that from the plantation to the border, from the genocide in Palestine to the Taliban’s war on women, and from refugee camps to the war on Iran, we encounter recurring attempts to preserve regimes of truth and imaginaries that seek to define the limits of life, mobility and freedom. Yet these projects of domination continually generate their own negation. Wherever people are confined, displaced, silenced or rendered disposable, fugitive forms of knowledge, pedagogy and imagination emerge. This is why history never ends.

Author’s note: a version of this essay’s opening story appears in my book ‘Illegal Traveller’: An Auto-Ethnography of Borders (2010) and in The Funambulist magazine.

Recent findings suggest that I take my holiday gift shopping very seriously — if not for my giftee, for my own serotonin-seeking purposes. There’s nothing quite as satisfying as finding the right N/A cocktail bundle for your aunt, or a cake stand that doubles as a chip and dip bowl (the in-laws will love that one) for the avid entertainer.

We’re all on different budgets; some are on the hunt for tasty bargains and piggy-bank-friendly stocking stuffers, while others have a more robust chunk of change set aside for providing big-impact presents You might have already bookmarked Eater’s gift guides that are under-$25, which is full of all kinds of chic home and kitchen goods, but now [turns up gas] we’re shopping at the under-$100 range, which gives us even more wiggle room to sweep your giftees off their feet via a ham-themed ornament, a robust at-home chai kit, or a set of steak knives from Peter Luger.

We’re in prime gift guide season, folks. Fasten your aprons, and let’s shop for every kind of food-loving person on your holiday list.

It has been revealed that no cocktail has been living, laughing, and loving harder than the ultra-dirty martini lately. This briny bundle from Significant Night brings together the shoppy shop’s sleek olive-themed hors d’oeuvres picks with a jar of Quincy’s big, juicy Castelvetrano olives, Quincy cocktail onions, and bag of Filthy’s cult-fave olive brine.

Significant Night Stock the Bar Gift Set.

For my money, a solid indicator of a fun household is whether or not there’s a wild cheese or cutting board in the mix. This psychedelic slab from Fredericks and Mae is both a beautiful serving board and functional chopping block for all of your kitchen needs, because it’s made out of a durable and non-toxic HDPE material.

Fredericks and Mae Red/Blue Cutting Board.

The organic Los Angeles lifestyle brand Flamingo Estate has created the pasta-lover’s dream present: a chic trio of pomodoro rosso sauce, angel trumpet pasta, and a bottle of Flamingo Estate’s heritage EVOO. As with the rest of the Estate’s bundles, this set comes housed in one of its signature, ornate green boxes.

Flamingo Estate Savory Festivo Pasta Set.

Industry observers note that imagine the flex of sawing through a Porterhouse at home with Peter Luger logo-stamped blades, which are made with stainless steel and wood handles that will transport their giftee back to the hallowed halls of the world-famous Brooklyn steakhouse. If you have a bit more room left in your gift budget, I suggest pairing it with some Newly introduced York strip steaks from Snake River Farms.

Diaspora Spice Co. is one of Eater’s favorite places to buy spices online, because it’s home to dozens of single-origin heirloom spices from (mostly) India and Sri Lanka. As founder Sana Javeri Kadri explains on its site, a core tenant of Diaspora Spice Co.’s operations is rooted in undoing colonialist inequity in the spice trade; in her words: “We’re proud to pay our farm partners an average of 6x above the commodity price. In a system where fair trade is a mere 15 percent premium, we pay what we believe to be a living wage.” The equitable spice brand has partnered with the North Carolina-based pottery and lifestyle brand East Fork on this at-home chai bundle, which features the former’s brand latest masala chai blend, Madhur jaggery, a stainless steel strainer, and a panna cotta colorway kuhlad from the indie pottery organization.

According to recent reports, eater’s deputy brand director Nat Belkov introduced me to Craighill, a tech giant that reimagines everyday carry and home essentials (think, scissors and carabiners) with a little more design flair. The Brooklyn-based studio redesigned the common wine key, and Belkov tells me that it mitigates all the annoying little things that can go wrong while using a wine opener. “I love the perfect angle on the foil cutter,” he claims, “[and] I love that they tapped the knowledge of sommelier André Hueston Mack to make sure it worked well enough to be trusted by members of the industry. Seldom do I run into a product where I genuinely have a hard time choosing between different color variations like here, with the sleek matte black, pop of orange, or classy tortoise finish. But most of all, I love that this thing is guaranteed to work for life.”.

MoMA Design Store Bodum Neon Nesting Mixing Bowls (Set of 4).

Industry observers note that as a person who drinks coffee every day (and feels horrified when I run out), I would be thrilled to receive this American Girl doll-sized bag (weighing 4 pounds) of beans from the award-winning Joshua Tree Coffee. This year, the Massive Bag — which is filled with the beans of your choice — even comes with a cute enamel mug.

Joshua Tree Coffee Massive Bag & Bellied Enamel Mug Bundle.

Japanese Taste Chitose Induction Compatible Japanese Stainless Steel Kettle.

These pastel eggnog petit fours come from the acclaimed Los Angeles-based confectionary Valerie Confections, and are made of a rich spiced buttercake, with bourbon ganache layers dipped in white chocolate and garnished with 23-karat gold leaf and chocolate biscuit pearls.

Recent findings suggest that ghia’s apéritif box is one of those drink-themed holiday gifts that sells out every year, because it pairs the brand’s signature amaro-esque N/A ambrosia with chic glassware from French-American glass artist and designer Sophie Lou Jacobsen. Whether you’re shopping for someone who doesn’t drink or is just trying to drink less alcohol in the new year, it’s a fashionable foot forward in the world of booze-free drinks.

Owning a double burner griddle is the culinary equivalent to flexing a California king size bed, because it can handle all of the pancakes, eggs, and grilled cheese orders from the family (without having to hop between skillets like a stove DJ). We love this one from Lodge, known for its excellent cast iron cookware.

Lodge Blacklock Triple Seasoned Cast Iron Double Burner Griddle.

Eater collaborated with heritage crystal glassware firm Zwiesel Fortessa on a collection of timeless pieces, including this versatile set of six Nick and Nora-style glasses.

Eater x Zwiesel Fortessa Folly Crystal Glass, 6 Ounce Cocktail (Set of 6).

Sometimes the best present is one that contains even more presents: a giant box of Swedish candies, all curated by the cult-fave confectioners at BonBon. According to recent reports, kudos to Emma Chamberlain on this postmodern-feeling French press. The YouTuber went viral yet again for her collaboration with West Elm, and this coffee press in particularly takes notes from its elders (Bodum and Alessi) with its sleek stainless steel design.

Emma Chamberlain x West Elm Stainless Steel Button French Press.

#4. 5 Cozy Meals Our Editors Make With Boxed Stuffing

5 Cozy Meals Our Editors Make With Boxed Stuffing

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Each month in Well Stocked, our staff shares unfussy recipe ideas that you can call upon any day of the week.
  • According to recent reports, few Thanksgiving dishes inspire as many strong opinions as stuffing slash dressing.
  • And then there’s a particularly resourceful subset of boxed-stuffing devotees: the maximalists who see the box as a pantry staple, not just a holiday shortcut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Each month in Well Stocked, our staff shares unfussy recipe ideas that you can call upon any day of the week. Because yes, our editors love to cook, but sometimes we need to get dinner on the table 12 minutes ago. That’s when we look to pantry and fridge staples that can quickly morph into delicious meals. This month, it’s all about boxed stuffing.

According to recent reports, few Thanksgiving dishes inspire as many strong opinions as stuffing slash dressing. In a baking dish or the bird itself? Sourdough or white bread? Fresh herbs or dried? Sausage or nah? There are the purists, who insist on drying their own bread, chopping aromatics, and seasoning everything from scratch. Then there are the Stove Top loyalists, who grew up on that unmistakable red box and remain fiercely faithful. Site director Rachel Tepper Paley is firmly in the latter camp. “My late father considered boxed Stove Top the Platonic ideal of stuffing, so I grew up with the uber-savory stuff on every Thanksgiving table,” she says. “We continue to serve it every year in his honor.”.

And then there’s a particularly resourceful subset of boxed-stuffing devotees: the maximalists who see the box as a pantry staple, not just a holiday shortcut. Our editors happen to be among them. Read on for all the ways they’re thinking outside the box.

Recent findings suggest that the first time I tried my colleague Jesse Szewczyk’s Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet in the Test Kitchen, I immediately started plotting all the occasions I could make it: Friendsgiving, a random Tuesday, football Sunday, date night. Its deliciousness caught me off guard. Jesse sears chicken thighs until golden and crisp, then uses the schmaltzy drippings (a.k.a liquid gold) to season the boxed stuffing. Dotted with sweet-tart cranberry gems, then baked with the chicken nestled back in, it’s basically Thanksgiving in one pan—and a recipe I blueprint to make well beyond November. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

When I find myself with instant stuffing, I like to make a baked eggs situation. I’ll make the stuffing according to the box’s directions in a shallow, oven-proof skillet. With the heat on (so the stuffing continues to crisp), I’ll toss in some greens like kale or spinach until they’re just barely wilted. Then, I’ll use a spatula to make a couple divots throughout and crack an egg into each. From there, I’ll pop the skillet into a 375°F oven and bake until the whites are set, about 15 minutes. A drizzle of green hot sauce and some salty feta crumble or sliced avocado, and I’m ready to eat. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor.

The way I see it, boxed stuffing mix is really close to a box of well-seasoned breadcrumbs. So why not use it as a savory panade that transforms lean ground turkey into tender meatballs? Senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk called this sheet-pan dinner Turkey and Stuffing Meatballs, but it honestly delivers all the flavors of Thanksgiving in one simple meal. You’ve got creamy baby Yukon gold potatoes and snappy green beans, plus a dipping sauce made from another autumn pantry staple, canned cranberry sauce, with lemon and honey to serve alongside. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

As a person who works in food media, I end up with my fair share of “what can I do with this?” ingredients. So while I firmly believe that no Thanksgiving dressing matters as much as my classic cornbread and biscuit version, I am no stranger to boxed stuffing. Frequently, it becomes a crust for baked fish. I’ve used Anna Stockwell’s easy no-recipe-required crispy fish method dozens of times since it first published, and it never disappoints. Best of all, you can use whatever bits and bobs you have lying around to build out the meal, and it’s relatively hands-off. Wins all around. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking.

Sources indicate that for cozy season, there is nothing more comforting than carbs on carbs. I’ve always loved pasta with breadcrumbs (every which way), but leave it to senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk to make that classic combo even better: In this recipe, instead of using plain breadcrumbs or Italian seasoned ones, he swaps in stuffing mix blitzed in the food processor. Brilliant. It’s a highly flavorful topping for pasta with sausage and kale, a total delight for a cold night. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Photo Credit: Large number of Americans are expected to hit the road for Thanksgiving this year. Pexels / Marta Wave.

This year’s gas prices are high enough to dent Thanksgiving travel plans, according to newly introduced research from AAA.

Higher fuel prices are pushing more travelers to stay home this Thanksgiving, according to a upcoming report from AAA.

The auto club projects 81.5 million Americans to travel at least 50 miles from home between November 24 and 30, down 0.1% from 81.6 million last year.

It’s a small dip, but excluding 2020, it’s the first time since the 2008 recession that AAA has reported a decline in its Thanksgiving travel projection. (Older projections measured a shorter travel window and are not directly comparable.).

According to recent reports, the decline was smaller than AAA anticipated, with nearly a quarter of the U.S. population still planning to travel, according to spokesperson Aixa Diaz,.

Industry observers note that the past year has been one of “Great Chickenings” and fine dining flips, British food invasions and restaurants whose dining rooms feel like living rooms, vibrant global steakhouses and unserious Y2K food. Among the slate of our 2026 Eater Award winners — which also brought undeniable new chef talent, core-memory-forming dishes, and groundbreaking bakeries and bars — are the places we could not stop thinking about for highly specific reasons. While this crop of restaurants and bars did not make the ultimate cut for the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, they commanded enough attention during our expansive scouting and research months to deserve acknowledgment. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

According to recent reports, cabbage is having its moment. From a star turn on the Sandy Liang runway as a ruffled bag to a hand-painted Bordallo Pinheiro dinner set and a declaration from Vogue that the leafy green has gone “chic,” the cruciferous vegetable is 2026’s “it” girl. The cult of the cabbage has made its way to Monte’s in Montecito, a cozy Korean American bistro where cone cabbage gets coal-roasted and kissed with salty smoked shiitake XO, an umami-heavy spin on the Hong Kong-born sauce. The fall-apart-tender cabbage beds on creamy tofu puree, the whole thing studded with hazelnuts that bring out the vegetable’s innate sweetness. Preparations like the one at Monte’s make it feel as though cabbage isn’t just this year’s distinguished vegetable — its dominance is here to stay. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest.

Maybe it was the Negroni, the Old Fashioned, and the gingery mezcal-laced Missed Opportunity. Perhaps it was the jetlag (who can say for sure?), but the bathroom at Bobo — the Filipino bar attached to Muhajir in Chicago’s Lincoln Park — left a lasting impression on me. In a world that’s fully embraced the bathroom selfie, Bobo has answered the call with refractory horizontal-mirrored panel walls and colored light that shifts from reds to greens, turning this lavatory into a mesmerizing disco ball. It’s a fitting touch that matches chef Jacob Dela Cruz’s vision for a red-light district-esque tropical hideaway. — Brenna Houck, Eater editorial manager.

Recent findings suggest that in a world of outrageous martinis, the one at Greenpoint Malaysian restaurant Kelang earns its playful name. The Dirty Fish riffs on a Vesper with gin, vodka, dry vermouth, and, saliently, fish sauce, which levels up the drink’s savoriness in every way. The pungent condiment mimics olive brine, delivering a salty taste of the sea to the already strong drink, which then gets garnished with wavy scallions and a long sliver of aromatic ginger. The cocktail showcases owner Chris Low’s background as a Malaysian kid who grew up in Newly introduced York. It’s simply presented — a cloudy drink in a stemmed coupe glass with those gloating garnishes — and pairs best with that fluffy paratha served over creamy and spicy dal. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York.

It has been revealed that gone may be the days of business power lunches at Wolfgang Puck’s Spago or Grill on the Alley that required a suit and tie. In their place, a latest arrangement has emerged — the low-key power lunch. There may be no better place for the midday meal masquerading as a meeting right now than at Little Fish in Melrose Hill, the first full-service restaurant from the former pop-up-turned-fish sandwich window. The light-filled dining room hums during daytime with flexibly scheduled creatives and well-dressed parents toting young children, all adults in the room sipping wine picked by sommelier Kae Whalen. On the menu, a tuna melt from maverick chefs and owners Anna Sonenshein and Niki Vahle will convert even nonbelievers, especially when paired with peppery fries dunked in horseradish aioli. Of course, there is the calling card fried fish sandwich, but smarter diners go for the beach sandwich layered with guindilla peppers and soy-cured mussels and a bay leaf chip stracciatella flecked with chocolate chips. Melrose Hill and its confluence of independent restaurants has morphed into a miniature walkable neighborhood — the perfect place to see and be seen. And what’s more low-key power lunch than that? — RR.

Sources indicate that historically, California is a gold mine of kitsch restaurants, from Clifton’s Republic to the pillowy pink dining room at the Madonna Inn. Night Hawk is the next jewel in that camp crown; the Greek-influenced San Diego restaurant is an anchor of Coronado Island’s hypermaximalist new Baby Grand hotel and beckons diners into a lush, faux-rock-filled outdoor dining room with pink clamshell chairs, waterfalls, and cocktails that have names like the Adonis in Bloom and Spanakopita Punch. In short: Tony Duquette by way of an acid tab. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

British food hit a fever pitch nationally this year as Americans awakened to the allure of meat pies and mushy peas. But if any restaurant truly dispelled notions of the country’s cuisine as dull or bland, it was Ambassadors Clubhouse, with its extensive menu of Punjabi showstoppers such as seven-layer, aloo-filed, Amritsari-style samosas; butter chicken in the form of lollipop-like chops with a heady char; and matka Beliram lamb, its crimson oil heralding intense flavor. In opulent, velvet-adorned surroundings that feel like a hideaway from the city, this luxe London import deliciously makes the case that Indian food is as essential to British cuisine as fish and chips. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

In a recent development, the most beautiful fresh restaurant in California is tucked into a shopping center in Montecito’s tony upper village. Little Mountain, which opened in November 2025 under chef Diego Moya, gives more to the scene than just a locavore menu that leans into live-fire cooking — it brings a bona fide, Architectural Digest-worthy destination that I would get married (and remarried) in. It may be hard to decide which room to sit in should you land a reservation in time: the comfortable dining room with gold-veil natural lighting and plush caramel booths and banquettes; the larger-party table that foregrounds an open kitchen and its centerpiece hearth; the dim, dark bar that may be the sexiest sliver of drinking den on the Central Coast; the covered patio that leads into a monarchial private dining area; or the outdoor patio that evokes dining in a home garden. Anywhere you sit, you can’t go wrong, especially as the food starts landing in front of you. — NF.

It has been revealed that chef Theo Adley opened Heretík last spring, and it has brought a breath of fresh, San Sebastián-esque sea breeze air into the Denver dining scene. The French- and Basque-leaning restaurant serves an endless summer menu of dishes like Santa Barbara uni, a playful pan con tomate martini, and scallops à la plancha with bearnaise and seaweed. The menu’s coastal Euro allure gets amplified by its interior design choices, which sprinkle in vintage furniture and tapered, wax drip-laden candles — but with a name like Heretík, you know that all of that romance is going to come with a healthy dose of cheek. — FK.

Chickens, you can’t take credit for this one: The British-inspired pub Dean’s proved that bigger is not always better with its take on a Scotch egg, which employs quail eggs instead of the typical chicken ones. In larger Scotch eggs, what appears in each bite can be inconsistent. But the result of the shrunken-down approach here is a reliably favorable ratio of meat to egg, in which each bite at once encompasses crunchy breading, tender meat filling, runny yolk, and just enough still-bouncy egg white. It’s as nonnegotiable at Dean’s as a pint of Guinness. — BM.

Ladyfish in Portland, Maine, has been clear about one thing since the beginning: “A summer fling,” the restaurant declared when it announced its May 2026 arrival. Jordan and Marisa Rubin of Portland sushi spot Mr. Tuna convinced chef Christine Lau to relocate from Upcoming York City to helm the seasonal seafood pop-up. Lau, whose resume includes Japanese-Italian and Chino Latino restaurants, brings her distinctive flair to classic Maine ingredients for dishes like scallops in a blanket with fried milk bread and the showstopping twin lobster mountain served with fries, rice cakes, and dan dan au poivre sauce. True to its word, the restaurant closed at the end of October. Here’s hoping the return of next year’s summertime crowds also brings back this match made in seafood heaven. — Stephanie Wu, editor in chief.

Industry observers note that los Angeles-born chef Ray Garcia opened Broken Spanish Comedor in Culver City in late 2025, years after his groundbreaking Mexican fine dining restaurant, Broken Spanish, and more casual B.S. Taqueria closed in Downtown Los Angeles. Garcia’s contribution to Alta California cuisine, rooted in Mexican cooking told through a California lens, remains one of the most distinct of this generation of restaurants. Still, he manages to surprise both longtime fans and newcomers to his work: The Comedor, whose name nods to the Indigenous homestyle restaurant tradition in Mexico, feels fresh in its A-frame home. It’s not uncommon for locals and those working in Los Angeles hospitality to stop in for a meal of crispy, crown-whorled chicharron or quesillo-threaded refried lentils; a classics-leaning drinks menu (cócteles, cervezas, vino) keeps the room humming happily. In a year brimming with significant restaurant comebacks (see also: Venice’s resurrected Tasting Kitchen and Keith Corbin’s reframed Alta Adams), it feels good to have an Angeleno chef like Ray Garcia capture our collective imagination again. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest.

If ever there was a destination in need of effective hangover cures, it’s New Orleans. While I was totally ready to rally after a two-bar, two-restaurant evening the night before (I am, of course, a professional), I also wasn’t mad about consuming something fortifying at Casimiro, the charming all-day cafe from award-winning Acamaya chef Ana Castro, the next morning. The restaurant delivered: textbook chilaquiles, impossibly fluffy conchas, crispy pescaditos, and one of the best tortas I’ve ever had. If hair of the dog is in your future in the City That Always Drinks, go with the well-balanced Cynar daiquiri to finish. — Missy Frederick, dining editorial director.

The weirdest thing I ate on a pastry this year was “lettuce cream” lacquered onto the BLT Danish at Dahlia in Minneapolis. The chartreuse-colored cream anchored a slice of late-August tomato and dollops of bacon jam atop persistently crisp laminated dough. One bite was enough to make me think, This should be more of a thing. You wouldn’t know at first glance that this bakery, tucked into an office complex, turns out treats of this caliber: jam-filled croissants with speculoos crumble, unassumingly perfect English muffins, plush milk bread and fluffy focaccia for sandwiches. This kind of out-of-the-box baking makes eating pastries right now so fun. — BM.

India’s Visa Overhaul Fixes the Easy Part of Its Tourism Problem

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, photo Credit: Passport control at Indira Gandhi International Airport in Delhi, India. Adobe Stock / saiko3p.

India’s visa changes remove one hurdle for foreign visitors. But an easier visa alone won’t bring more tourists or get India close to its target of 100 million visitors.

India has simplified its visa system, cutting the number of main categories from 13 to nine and reducing the information required on application forms by as much as 70%, as the government looks to make entry easier for foreign visitors.

The revised system should go live by the end of 2026, the country’s home ministry said.

It is the second overhaul of the visa regime in 13 months. The home ministry said it has also reduced the number of sub-categories from 49 to 23, following an earlier consolidation in October 2025.

In a recent development, the changes come as India struggles to revive inbound tourism even as the government targets 100 million visitors by 2047. The country received 9.2 million foreign tourists in 2025, down 9.4% from 2024 and about 16% below its pre-pandemic peak of 10.9 million in 2019. The overhaul addresses longstanding complaints that India’s visa process is needlessly complicated for ordinary tourists.

Government think tank NITI Aayog flagg.
